examples: Students classified as low initial ability received two days of whole-class plus two days of small-group Fluency Formula™ instruction weekly
key_sources: Fluency Formula™ WWC Intervention Report. (2007). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://teacher.scholastic.com/products/fluencyformula/pdfs/FF_EffectivessReport.pdf

article_title: Stepping Stones to Literacy (Beginning Reading)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Stepping Stones to Literacy. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.steppingstonestoliteracy.com
title: Model-lead-test lesson format with progress monitoring and re-teaching
description: Each SSL lesson sequences four to six activities and follows a model-lead-test format: "The teacher first models the target skill. Students replicate the example and practice the skill with assistance from the teacher." Teachers then monitor student progress and re-teach skills to students who do not fully master them, and lessons can be repeated to support mastery. Each lesson begins with a set of nursery rhymes before the sequenced instructional activities.
requirements: Teacher guides students through the sequenced activities and monitors progress to decide when re-teaching is needed
target_learners: Kindergarten and older preschool students with early literacy deficits
target_learning_goals: Mastery of five critical early literacy skill sets
examples: SSL's 25 lessons each begin with nursery rhymes and use the model-lead-test format with re-teaching for students who do not fully master a skill.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Stepping Stones to Literacy. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.steppingstonestoliteracy.com

article_title: Read, Write & Type! (Beginning Reading)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Read, Write & Type!™. http://www.fcrr.org/TechnicalReports/RWTfullrept.pdf
title: Writing-to-read lesson sequence with speed-practice and simulated e-mail activities
description: The program's instructional pattern moves from sound-level to text-level production: lessons "begin by having students say and write individual sounds and the letters that represent those sounds, and then progress to having students write words, sentences, and stories." Two supplementary activities extend the pattern: the Power Fountain activity for practicing "speed and accuracy in writing and typing" after attaining a certain level, and the E-mail Tower, "a simulated e-mail program," for practicing newly acquired skills by writing short messages. Teachers or parents can print individual or group progress reports.
requirements: The software plus corresponding activity book lessons; a teacher or parent able to print progress reports; computer access at school or home
constraints: Speed and accuracy practice via the Power Fountain activity is available only after students attain a certain level; the E-mail Tower is described as optional
target_learners: Beginning readers aged six to nine
target_learning_goals: Sounding out, typing, and writing words, sentences, and stories
examples: The evaluated implementation paired teacher-led warm-up activities from the teacher's manual with individual computer practice of the same skills
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Read, Write & Type!™. http://www.fcrr.org/TechnicalReports/RWTfullrept.pdf
grain_size: lesson-to-unit sequence within a software curriculum

article_title: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (BCIRC) (English Language Learners)
citation: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition. (2007). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED405428
title: BCIRC before-, during-, and after-reading activity structure
description: BCIRC organizes instruction as a recurring cycle of fifteen activities occurring before, during, and after reading. As the report describes, "Fifteen activities occur before, during, and after reading, including using BCIRC materials to develop vocabulary, making predictions of a story's content based on its title, and reading with a partner followed by silent reading". Teachers model reading strategies such as making and confirming a prediction before, during, and after reading, and cooperative groups then apply the demonstrated strategy while attempting to comprehend stories from their classroom text. The pattern embeds vocabulary, prediction, partner reading, and writing within cooperative teams.
requirements: Teachers combine CIRC strategies with transitional and English as a Second Language strategies
Extensive staff development on facilitating cooperative learning discussions
constraints: Designed for students transitioning from Spanish primary-language reading instruction in grades 2-5
target_learners: Elementary English language learners whose primary home language is Spanish
target_learning_goals: Cooperative discussion and academic English use
examples: In the reviewed study, teachers modeled strategies such as making and confirming a prediction, and cooperative groups then applied the demonstrated strategy while attempting to comprehend stories selected from their classroom text
key_sources: Bilingual Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition. (2007). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED405428

article_title: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates (VIP) (English Language Learners)
citation: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.brookespublishing.com/store/books/lively-6342/index.htm
title: Weekly vocabulary cycle: native-language preview, English introduction, small-group word tasks, and word-analysis Friday
description: VIP organizes instruction as a repeating weekly cycle around a weekly reading assignment. "On Mondays English language learner students are given the weekly reading assignment in their native language to preview before it is introduced in English on the following day." Tuesdays bring whole-group lessons defining target vocabulary; Wednesdays use heterogeneous language groups for two cloze activities; Thursdays use small groups for word association, synonym/antonym, and semantic feature analysis; Fridays cover root-word analysis and multiple meanings of words.
requirements: Bilingual capacity or materials to provide the native-language (Spanish) preview on Monday
Heterogeneous grouping based on English language proficiency for mid-week activities
constraints: Evaluated in grades 4-6 with Spanish-speaking English language learners in bilingual and mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: word meaning, morphology, and multiple meanings
examples: In the study, three lessons observed during weeks 4, 9, and 13 revealed six of nine intervention teachers implemented more than 70% of key lesson elements
key_sources: Vocabulary Improvement Program for English Language Learners and Their Classmates. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.brookespublishing.com/store/books/lively-6342/index.htm

article_title: Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs (English Language Learners)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs — WWC Intervention Report. http://crede.berkeley.edu/research/crede/research/llaa/1.5pubs.html
title: Alternating literature log writing and teacher-facilitated discussion around the same story
description: In the short-term implementation, the two components were "used on alternating days with the same story". Learners first wrote log entries about personal experiences relevant to a character, descriptions of story events, and evaluations of a theme, writing independently and then joining a teacher-led discussion comparing their experiences to the character's. Instructional Conversation lessons then involved teacher-facilitated small-group discussions of story content, approximately 45 minutes per week, giving teachers an opportunity to assess comprehension and broaden understanding of themes.
requirements: Teachers act as discussion facilitators rather than lecturers
Log prompts tied to segments of the same story being discussed
constraints: In the reviewed short-term study the comparison group received less teacher-led instructional time, which confounded the intervention's effects
examples: Learners spent at least 45 minutes creating an illustration and caption summarizing their interpretation of the story "Louella's Song" in both intervention and comparison conditions.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). Instructional Conversations and Literature Logs — WWC Intervention Report. http://crede.berkeley.edu/research/crede/research/llaa/1.5pubs.html

article_title: Too Good For Violence (TGFV) (Character Education)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Violence. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mendezfoundation.org
title: Scripted lessons combining role-playing, cooperative learning games, small group activities, and classroom discussion
description: The program's lesson design pattern pairs fully scripted lessons with active, participatory methods. As the report describes, "All lessons are scripted and engage students through role-playing and cooperative learning games, small group activities, and classr oom discussions." Cooperative learning activities, role-playing, and skill building methods reinforce positive behaviors and skills and encourage students to apply them in other contexts. Lessons run 30-60 minutes in elementary school and 30-45 minutes in middle school.
requirements: Scripted lessons are intended to be taught by trained teachers or Mendez Foundation instructors.
examples: Lessons include peaceful conflict resolution strategies and prosocial skill development in goal setting, decisionmaking, anger and stress management, communication, and peer resistance.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Violence. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mendezfoundation.org

article_title: Enhanced Proactive Reading (English Language Learners)
citation: Enhanced Proactive Reading. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Supplemental small-group daily reading instruction pattern for struggling first-grade English learners
description: The intervention pattern evaluated in both trials is daily supplemental reading instruction delivered in small groups of three to five students with homogeneous reading achievement, in a pull-out setting, as an addition to the core reading program. Each 50-minute lesson combines about 40 minutes of lesson delivery with 10 minutes of oracy practice, and activities include word games for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence practice, letter writing, and learning new letter sounds. Instructors "provide opportunities for participation from all students and give feedback for student responses", with largely choral student responses, teacher modeling of new content, and fast-paced lessons monitored for progress.
requirements: Teachers receive 12 hours of professional development before implementation and six additional hours six weeks after the start, plus frequent staff development sessions and on-site coaching
Delivered as a supplement to the regular reading instruction, not a replacement for it
constraints: Evaluated only with first-grade Hispanic English language learners in Texas schools at risk for reading problems
In the Vaughn, Mathes, et al. (2006) trial, comparison students received an average of 63.7 hours of supplemental instruction from other sources, with wide variability
target_learners: First-grade English language learners scoring below the 25th percentile in early reading
target_learning_goals: Early reading skills: phonemic awareness, letter knowledge, word recognition, text fluency, and comprehension strategies
examples: Both reviewed trials implemented the pattern from October to May in four Texas schools each, with fidelity checked via checklists and observations and found acceptable
key_sources: Enhanced Proactive Reading. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Green Dot Public Schools
citation: Green Dot Public Schools. (2018). WWC Intervention Report: Green Dot Public Schools, Charter Schools. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.greendot.org
title: Large high school divided into multiple small charter schools as a turnaround design
description: This whole-school design pattern converts one existing, underperforming public high school into a set of smaller autonomous charter schools sharing the same neighborhood catchment. The reviewed study "examined a group of Green Dot Public Schools formed by dividing an existing public high school into a set of smaller schools": the original school was divided into two off-site small schools in the first year and into eight schools by the second year, serving the full prior student community. The pattern pairs small-school community with the charter operator's six-principle model.
requirements: Chartering and district authorization to convert an existing district-run school
Funding for transformation operations, which in the reported case came largely from private foundations
constraints: Evidence for the pattern comes from one quasi-experimental study meeting WWC standards with reservations in a single urban district
target_learners: Ninth-through-twelfth-grade students in an underperforming urban high school catchment
target_learning_goals: Improved achievement, attendance, and graduation in a turnaround setting
examples: Green Dot started converting the LAUSD school with two off-site small schools in 2007–08 and reached eight schools by fall 2008, spending approximately $15 million over a 4-year turnaround
key_sources: Lb0

article_title: Lessons in Character (Character Education)
citation: Lessons in Character. (2006). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.youngpeoplespress.com
title: Theme-of-the-week character lesson structure with story introduction and varied activities
description: The curriculum uses a recurring weekly instructional pattern: a 'theme of the week' approach in which the teacher introduces the week's concept by reading stories portraying that value in action, then engages students in targeted activities, with a class project centered on the lesson's main idea. Supplemental materials support daily oral language development and weekly writing assignments designed to enhance understanding of the week's core concept. This structure integrates literacy activities with character value instruction.
requirements: Teacher's guide providing the lesson's main idea, concrete objectives, and teaching strategies; binders with strategies, skills, suggestions, and techniques
constraints: The reviewed studies used only the classroom materials; the authors note comprehensive character education would involve administrators, parents, and others on campus
target_learners: elementary school students (grades 4-5 in the reviewed studies)
examples: Teachers introduce the week's concept, read stories portraying that value in action, and engage students in targeted activities
key_sources: Lessons in Character. (2006). WWC Intervention Report, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/WWC/InterventionReport/270

article_title: Too Good for Drugs (TGFD) (Character Education)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Drugs. https://www.mendezfoundation.org
title: Skill-building lesson pattern combining cooperative learning, role-play, and application across contexts for social and resistance skills
description: The program's lesson design pattern pairs explicit instruction in named skills with active practice formats: "Instructional strategies cover goal setting and decisionmaking skills, prosocial skills, resistance to negative peer influence skills, and interpersonal skills." Within each scripted lesson, "Cooperative learning activities, role-play, and skill-building methods reinforce positive behaviors and skills and encourage students to apply these behaviors and skills in other contexts." The pattern embeds character values (respect for self and others, empathic responding, responsibility) into most lessons rather than teaching them separately, and lessons include information about drug use frequency and harmful effects.
requirements: Scripted lessons delivered by trained teachers or program instructors
Grade-level kits including student workbooks and lesson extenders
constraints: Evaluated as a classroom-based (not schoolwide) intervention in the reviewed studies
examples: Students engaged in role-play and cooperative learning games and were encouraged to apply the skills to different contexts across the 10 scripted lessons at each grade level
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Drugs. https://www.mendezfoundation.org

article_title: DaisyQuest (Early Childhood Education)
citation: DaisyQuest for Preschool Children. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Story-framed mastery-based computer activities with reward clues
description: DaisyQuest organizes phonological awareness practice as levels embedded in a fairy-tale narrative, where mastering each level yields clues advancing the story. The report states: "As children master each level of instructional activities, they are rewarded with clues that eventually lead them to discover where Daisy is hiding." The same structure recurs in Daisy's Castle, where completing levels yields clues to lost eggs, and "DaisyQuest uses story lines and colorful graphics to engage children in the learning process."
requirements: Instructional activities organized into mastery levels with an overarching narrative providing reward clues
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness skills practiced through game-like mastery levels
examples: DaisyQuest's search for the dragon Daisy and Daisy's Castle's search for Daisy's lost eggs both link activity levels to narrative clues
key_sources: DaisyQuest for Preschool Children. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Fast ForWord® (English Language Learners)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Fast ForWord Language. http://www.scilearn.com
title: Continuously adaptive task difficulty targeting about 80% item success
description: In Fast ForWord Language, "The difﬁculty of each task is continuously adapted so that students would get about 80% of the items correct." Each of the seven exercises begins with basic skills and builds up to more complex skills, so learners work within an individually calibrated difficulty band maintained by continuous adaptation. This pattern keeps success rates near a target level while skills progress from simple to complex across the exercise sequence.
requirements: Computer-based exercises that can adjust item difficulty continuously during use
constraints: The 80% success target is stated as the design goal of this specific program's tasks
target_learning_goals: cognitive skills including memory, attention, processing, and sequencing
examples: Fast ForWord Language's seven game-like exercises each begin with basic skills and build up to more complex skills with continuously adapted difficulty
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Fast ForWord Language. http://www.scilearn.com
grain_size: task/exercise level within a computer-based instructional program

article_title: Reading Mastery (English Language Learners)
citation: WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery SRA/McGraw-Hill. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Reading Mastery lesson design: fast-paced scripted lessons with modeling, guided practice, and individual practice
description: Reading Mastery lessons are 'designed to be fast-paced and interactive,' using 30- to 45-minute lessons with seven to nine short activities spanning multiple content strands such as phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondence, sounding out words, word recognition, vocabulary, oral reading fluency, and comprehension. The overarching teaching routine repeated throughout the curriculum is composed of modeling new content, providing guided practice, and implementing individual practice and application. Lesson scripts guide teachers, and signals and group responses keep students involved and on task and control lesson pacing.
requirements: Lesson scripts act as a guide for teachers; delivery assistants received 10 hours of preservice training and were observed weekly in the first month and twice a month thereafter to ensure program standards.
target_learners: Beginning readers in grades K-6, including English language learners
target_learning_goals: Explicit, systematic beginning reading skills across phonemic awareness, decoding, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension strands
examples: A typical lesson includes seven to nine short activities that encompass multiple strands of content.
key_sources: WWC Intervention Report: Reading Mastery SRA/McGraw-Hill. (2006). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Early Risers
citation: Early Risers. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Children Classified as Having an Emotional Disturbance. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.med.umn.edu/psychiatry/research/earlyrisers/home.html
title: Four-component intervention model combining child skills, school support, parent skills, and family support
description: Early Risers organizes its intervention as four coordinated components. The Child Skills component teaches skills that enhance children's emotional and behavioral self-regulation, positive peer relationships, and academic success. The Child School Support component identifies areas of difficulty in the classroom and creates individualized plans addressed during normal school activities. The Parent Skills component is delivered in family night group sessions teaching positive parent-child relations, effective discipline, and school involvement, while the Family Support component uses home visits to identify basic needs and health concerns and implement plans for healthy lifestyles.
requirements: A family advocate coordinates the child- and family-focused components
Delivery across multiple years with both school-year and summer programming
target_learners: Elementary school children demonstrating early aggressive and disruptive behavior
examples: In August et al. (2003), the full-strength group received Child Skills components for two years plus the Family Support component, which included home-based therapy with a minimum of three bimonthly contacts in the first year and six contacts in the second year.
key_sources: Early Risers. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Children Classified as Having an Emotional Disturbance. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.med.umn.edu/psychiatry/research/earlyrisers/home.html

article_title: GEMS Space Science Sequence
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2012, June). Science intervention report: Great Explorations in Math and Science® (GEMS®) Space Science Sequence. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Reform-based space science unit pattern: models, hands-on investigations, peer discussion, and misconception-targeted activities
description: The GEMS® Space Science Sequence embodies a reform-based instructional pattern in which "The sequence utilizes models, hands-on investigations, peer-to-peer discussions, reflection, and informational student readings." Activities "target core space science concepts and common misconceptions that students might have about them", and students working in small groups "evaluate alternative explanations, use evidence to support them, and critique the merits of an explanation." Each unit builds on knowledge from previous units and can also be used independently.
requirements: Teacher professional development and implementation support as provided in the evaluated study
Small-group work structures for evaluating and critiquing explanations
constraints: In the evaluated trial, teachers in both groups were instructed to refrain from adding any activities to those present in their assigned curriculum
target_learning_goals: Core space science concepts and addressing common student misconceptions
Evaluating alternative explanations and using evidence in science
examples: The trial compared this pattern against a district curriculum centered on a more didactic presentation of space science concepts, including direct instruction, reading of text, and students answering very focused questions
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2012, June). Science intervention report: Great Explorations in Math and Science® (GEMS®) Space Science Sequence. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/612

article_title: Spelling Mastery
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2014, January). Students with Learning Disabilities intervention report: Spelling Mastery. Retrieved from http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Three-strategy spelling instruction pattern sequencing phonemic, morphemic, and whole-word approaches by skill development
description: Spelling Mastery organizes spelling instruction as a developmental sequence of three strategies matched to student skill level. Beginning students learn sound–symbol correspondence so they can "generalize these skills to spell word segments that follow regular patterns"; more advanced students learn to spell and blend bases and affixes (morphographs), which the report calls "most efficient for multisyllabic words that are not easy to spell phonemically"; and all students memorize common irregularly spelled words. Teachers integrate concepts cumulatively, with all strategies used and practiced over time, and introduce sound–spelling relationships, morphographs, rules, and principles in a scaffolded instructional sequence.
requirements: Requires scripted lessons organized according to students' skill development, with scaffolded steps so students finish each concept before a new one is presented
constraints: The morphemic strategy is described as most efficient for multisyllabic words that are not easy to spell phonemically; the whole-word strategy targets common words with irregular letter sounds
target_learners: Beginning spellers through more advanced elementary students in grades 1–6, including students with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Spelling regular-pattern words via sound–symbol correspondence, spelling multisyllabic words via morphographs, and memorizing irregular words
examples: In the 2006 RCT, Level D lessons were organized around a weekly word type (phonetically regular words, regular words with a prefix or suffix, irregular words) with rule introduction, rule application, and independent worksheet practice
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2014, January). Students with Learning Disabilities intervention report: Spelling Mastery. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/579

article_title: Red Light, Purple Light! (RLPL)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2022). Red Light, Purple Light. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Implement Red Light, Purple Light as short circle-time sessions twice weekly over eight weeks with trained teachers
description: In the studies contributing to the WWC report, the program was delivered in low-dosage, repeated circle-time sessions rather than as a separate curriculum block. Teachers implemented sessions "for approximately 20 minutes during circle time," and "The Red Light, Purple Light sessions took place twice a week for 8 weeks." Teachers implementing the sessions received a 3-hour in-person training and a developer-provided kit of materials; comparison teachers received no program training.
requirements: A half-day (3-hour) in-person training from the developer, plus a training manual and a materials kit.
constraints: The evidence comes from Head Start centers in the Pacific Northwest with children from families below the poverty threshold; effects on other populations are not established in this report.
target_learners: preschool children in Head Start classrooms
examples: Both qualifying studies used cluster randomized designs in which teachers were assigned to receive the training and implement the sessions or to continue with business as usual.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2022). Red Light, Purple Light. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/725

article_title: Open Court Reading©
citation: Open Court Reading©. (2014). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading, Updated October 2014. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://www.mheonline.com/
title: Three-part unit progression: Preparing to Read, Reading and Responding, Language Arts
description: Each unit of Open Court Reading© is organized into three parts in a logical progression. Part One, Preparing to Read, addresses phonemic awareness, sounds and letters, phonics, fluency, and word knowledge; Part Two, Reading and Responding, emphasizes reading literature for understanding, comprehension, inquiry, and practical reading applications; Part Three, Language Arts, focuses on writing, spelling, grammar, usage, mechanics, and basic computer skills. The pattern sequences skills instruction before and alongside literature-based application and written language work.
requirements: Grade-specific materials for each part, including the Teacher's Edition with lesson plans stating goals and objectives
constraints: Evaluated in this report only for grades K–3
examples: Part One of each unit, Preparing to Read, focuses on phonemic awareness, sounds and letters, phonics, fluency, and word knowledge
key_sources: Open Court Reading©. (2014). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading, Updated October 2014. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/347

article_title: Wilson Reading System®
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Wilson Reading System®. What Works Clearinghouse, Beginning Reading. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Daily 10-part lesson plan in three instructional blocks with built-in review
description: The Wilson Reading System organizes each lesson into "a daily 10-part lesson plan that builds on interaction between the teacher and student," divided into three blocks: parts one through five emphasize word study, parts six through eight emphasize spelling, and parts nine and 10 emphasize fluency and comprehension. The program sequences word-structure instruction from basic word skills to more complex language structure including morphological principles, with reviews reinforcing previous lessons. Lessons run 45–90 minutes in reading classes, small groups, or tutorials.
requirements: A Wilson instructors' manual that helps the teacher prepare the daily lesson
teacher-student interaction as the core of each lesson
constraints: The intensive model of 60–90 minute instruction in small groups or individually is recommended for the most challenged readers
target_learners: striving readers in grade 2 and above
examples: In the reviewed study, a 50-minute lesson was delivered five days a week to groups of three students with various basic reading levels
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: Wilson Reading System®. What Works Clearinghouse, Beginning Reading. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/546

article_title: Read Well® (English Language Learners)
citation: Read Well®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://store.cambiumlearning.com/resource.aspx?page=ProgramOverview&site=sw&parentId=019005451
title: Scaffold early reading instruction by modeling, then gradually decreasing teacher support toward independent performance
description: Read Well® is based on "the tenets of scaffolded instruction, in which teachers begin by presenting models and gradually decreasing their support by providing guided practice before students are asked to complete the skill or strategy independently". A concrete instantiation is shared reading of new text in which the teacher reads the difficult or irregular words; as student skills and motivation increase, the amount of teacher-read text decreases and the student gains greater independence. The program also lets pacing depend on each participant's level of mastery.
requirements: Teacher materials and guided practice structures that allow support to be faded as student skills increase
constraints: The report describes this as the program's design tenet; the reviewed evidence does not isolate scaffolding as the causal ingredient
target_learning_goals: independent application of skills and strategies
examples: Student and teacher read new text aloud with the teacher reading the difficult or irregular words, and the amount of teacher-read text decreases as student skills increase
key_sources: Read Well®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://store.cambiumlearning.com/resource.aspx?page=ProgramOverview&site=sw&parentId=019005451

article_title: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis
citation: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Staged progression from discrete trial training to naturalistic instruction and generalization
description: The Lovaas Model organizes instruction as a staged progression. "During the first stages of the intervention, the main method of teaching is discrete trial training", and "As children progress, therapists gradually increase the emphasis on instruction in less structured or more natural settings, such as peer play and classrooms." Early stages target reducing behaviors that interfere with learning and teaching prerequisite skills such as requesting, imitation, and following instructions; instruction then advances to expressive and receptive language, then social and conversation skills, and finally pre-academic and observational learning skills, with programming for generalization to preschool and community settings.
requirements: Trained one-to-one instructors, trainers, and supervisors delivering 35 to 40 hours per week of intervention
constraints: The intervention generally lasts about three years, beginning with children ages 18 to 42 months
target_learners: young children with autism or pervasive developmental disorder
target_learning_goals: prerequisite skills such as requesting and imitation
examples: A typical therapy session lasts two to three hours, with structured time devoted to tasks such as appropriate toy play or following instructions, followed by breaks used for incidental teaching or generalization activities
key_sources: Lovaas Model of Applied Behavior Analysis. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/295

article_title: Accelerated Middle Schools
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2008). WWC Intervention Report: Accelerated Middle Schools. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Accelerated middle schools share a common design: thematic cross-subject linking, experiential instruction, smaller classes, and added academic and social supports
description: Despite varying somewhat in instructional approach, the programs share several common design elements: "Classes are often linked thematically across multiple subjects"; instruction is "more experiential and 'hands on' than is typical in a traditional middle school"; classes are generally smaller than in traditional middle schools; and programs provide additional supports such as tutoring, attendance monitoring, counseling, and family outreach. This pattern describes the program-level configuration the three studied schools shared.
requirements: Additional instructional time in core academic subjects, obtained by offering relatively few electives
constraints: Programs vary somewhat in their approach to instruction; the pattern describes the three studied schools rather than all accelerated middle schools
target_learners: middle school students behind grade level
target_learning_goals: accelerated coverage of core academic curriculum
examples: The three School Dropout Demonstration Assistance Program sites in Georgia, Michigan, and New Jersey
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2008). WWC Intervention Report: Accelerated Middle Schools. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/11

article_title: Success for All®
citation: Success for All®. (2017). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.successforall.org/
title: SFA® ability-grouped 90-minute daily reading block with sequenced phonics-to-comprehension instruction
description: SFA® elementary reading programs "combine cooperative-learning strategies with detailed lessons, which incorporate multimedia, puppet skits, and videos to support students' engagement and classroom instruction." Students in prekindergarten through first grade participate in Reading Roots, and students in second grade and above participate in Reading Wings. Students are grouped into reading classes of 15–20 students with others of similar reading ability, regardless of age or grade level, during a daily 90-minute reading period; regrouping by demonstrated improvement lets teachers teach the whole class without smaller within-class groups. Instruction is sequenced across several years, emphasizing phonemic awareness initially and broader reading skills later, with daily tutoring for struggling readers.
requirements: Certified teachers or paraprofessionals to provide daily tutoring to students who have difficulty reading at the same level as their classmates
Regrouping structures that allow reading classes of 15–20 students of similar ability across age or grade levels
constraints: The review focuses on the literacy component implemented within the whole-school reform program, so most students also received other program components
target_learning_goals: phonemic awareness, phonics, listening and speaking vocabulary, reading comprehension, and composition writing
examples: Teachers begin the period by reading children's storybooks aloud and discussing them; in grades 2–5 teachers use structured interactive activities built around partner reading and cooperative learning
key_sources: Success for All®. (2017). WWC Intervention Report: Beginning Reading. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/672

article_title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD)
citation: Self-Regulated Strategy Development: WWC Intervention Report. (2017). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.thinksrsd.com
title: Teach self-regulation skills alongside academic strategies so students can apply strategies without guidance
description: SRSD pairs explicit instruction in a concrete academic strategy with instruction in self-regulation skills, so that students come to apply the strategy independently. The report states: "A key part of the process is teaching self-regulation skills, such as goal-setting and self-monitoring, which aim to help students apply the strategy without guidance." Teachers instruct students in monitoring and evaluating their strategy use, model both the strategy and self-regulation, and gradually transfer responsibility until students perform tasks without support.
requirements: Teachers provide support tailored to student needs, frequent constructive feedback, and positive reinforcement during the supported-practice stage.
constraints: The intervention begins with teacher direction and ends with students independently applying the strategy; effectiveness evidence in this report covers students with specific learning disabilities in grades 2 through 10.
target_learners: Students with learning disabilities in grades 2 through 12
target_learning_goals: Independent application of academic strategies such as essay planning and organizing ideas before writing
examples: In the model-the-strategy stage, teachers use a think-aloud process and voice positive self-statements; students set individual targets to improve on baseline performance.
key_sources: Self-Regulated Strategy Development: WWC Intervention Report. (2017). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/680

article_title: Good Behavior Game
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023). Good Behavior Game. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Team-based interdependent group contingency game structure
description: The Good Behavior Game follows a recurring session structure: "Teachers divided their students into teams and reviewed the expected behaviors and rules of the game. Teachers monitored student behavior during the game and scored the teams based on how well they followed the rules. At the end of the session, winning teams received a reward." Rules typically include staying seated and on task, following directions, being polite, and ignoring distractions, displayed on a poster. Teachers choose scoring methods (adding or subtracting points), constant or variable winning goals, and reward timing. Variations in the reviewed studies included a whole-class-as-one-team version and placing individual students on their own team.
requirements: Teachers describe and remind students of game rules and winning criteria before starting the game, as done in all 16 reviewed studies
Teachers provide rewards to winning teams, as done in all 16 reviewed studies
constraints: In the reviewed studies the game was played during the school day in 15 studies and in an after-school program in one study
target_learners: Students in grades K-11 classrooms, including whole classes and focal students with high levels of disruptive behavior
target_learning_goals: Reducing disruptive behavior and rule violations
examples: In six studies teachers offered winning students small prizes such as snacks, school supplies, stickers, or lip balm; in three studies teachers offered classroom privileges such as free time
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023). Good Behavior Game. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/728

article_title: Everyday Mathematics®
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Spiral curriculum structure: repeated reinforcement of concepts within and across grade levels
description: The curriculum's organizing structure is longitudinal revisiting of content: it "exposes students to material over extended periods of time by repeatedly reinforcing material both within and across grade levels." Program Goals "are organized by content strand and are the same at all grade levels," a structure that "interconnects the curriculum across grades and helps students build a solid base and consistently learn each skill and concept," with Grade-Level Goals specifying the content to master each year.
requirements: A stable set of Program Goals held constant across grade levels, refined into approximately 20–25 Grade-Level Goals per grade, so content can be revisited in varying instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: building a solid base of mathematics skills and concepts consistently across grades
examples: Concepts are reviewed and extended in varying instructional contexts across grade levels; basic skills practice recurs through written and oral fact practice, fluency activities, mental math, daily review problem sets, homework, and math games.
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/166

article_title: Everyday Mathematics®
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Balance teacher-directed instruction with open-ended problem solving, hands-on exploration, and varied skills practice in mathematics lessons
description: Everyday Mathematics® embodies balanced instruction: "Each lesson includes whole-class instruction and small-group, partner, or individual activities. This structure balances teacher-directed instruction with open-ended problem solving, hands-on explorations, long-term projects, and ongoing practice." Basic skills practice is provided through multiple methods, including "written and oral fact practice, fluency activities and tests, mental math activities, daily sets of review problems, homework assignments, and a variety of math games."
requirements: Lesson structures that pair whole-class teacher-led segments with small-group, partner, or individual activities, plus recurring practice opportunities across multiple formats
target_learning_goals: mathematics concepts, skills fluency, and real-life problem solving
examples: In the reviewed implementation, daily lesson plans usually began with a Math Message as the focus of the lesson, combining teacher-led discussions and hands-on group and individual activities, with student journals and homework reinforcing practical experience.
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2015, November). Primary Mathematics intervention report: Everyday Mathematics®. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/166

article_title: Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math
citation: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2013). Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Teacher-guided small-group manipulatives lessons paired with parallel take-home parent activities
description: The Pre-K Mathematics program organizes instruction as weekly math activities presented twice in teacher-guided small-group lessons of four to six children lasting approximately 20 minutes, using concrete manipulatives, with "related math activities... sent home every 1 to 2 weeks" and parents encouraged to engage their children with these activities. Home activity materials parallel the classroom activities and are available with picture strips in English or Spanish. This classroom-plus-home structure was implemented across both reviewed studies over the school year.
requirements: Teachers need the core program package (teacher's curriculum book, Activity Aid Masters, Home Activity Masters, and Assessment Record Sheets) and training; in the reviewed studies teachers received multi-day workshops and ongoing on-site training approximately twice per month.
constraints: The pattern was evaluated as a supplement to existing general curricula (The Creative Curriculum, High/Scope, Montessori, or local curricula), not as a stand-alone replacement.
target_learners: preschool children in Head Start and state-funded preschool classrooms
target_learning_goals: early mathematical knowledge in counting, arithmetic, geometry, patterns, measurement, and logical reasoning
examples: In the PCER study, 29 classroom activities were completed and teachers sent 19 home activities and materials for children to complete at home, with teachers completing Assessment Record Sheets tied to each session.
key_sources: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. (2013). Pre-K Mathematics with DLM Early Childhood Express Math. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/381
grain_size: lesson-to-unit level across a school year

article_title: SpellRead
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: SpellRead™. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Three-phase sequential skill-mastery structure for remedial reading instruction
description: SpellRead™ organizes instruction as "140 lessons implemented in three distinct phases that interweave phonemics, phonetics, and instruction in language-based reading and writing". Phase A (50 lessons) trains the auditory process to hear and manipulate the 44 sounds of English; Phase B (30 lessons) covers secondary vowel spelling, consonant blends, and two-syllable syllabication; Phase C (25 lessons) addresses decoding words of three or more syllables, clusters, and verb forms. Each lesson includes activities for phonemic, phonetic, semantic, syntactic, comprehension/vocabulary, and fluency skills.
requirements: Systematic and explicit instruction with specific skill mastery emphasized
Small-group delivery with one instructor
target_learners: Struggling readers in grades 2 or above
examples: Phase A (50 lessons) is designed to train the auditory process function of the brain to hear and manipulate the 44 sounds of the English language
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2007). WWC Intervention Report: SpellRead™. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc

article_title: Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition (CIRC) — Adolescent Literacy
citation: Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, Adolescent Literacy. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Cooperative paired and small-group literacy routines with team rewards
description: CIRC's instructional pattern organises daily lessons around cooperative structures: "Pairs of students read to each other; predict how stories will end; summarize stories; write responses to questions posed by the teacher; and practice spelling, decoding, and vocabulary". Within teams of four, mixed-ability students work on story main ideas and linked writing activities, and teams are rewarded on collective performance to motivate helping. The pattern integrates comprehension practice with the writing process on the texts students read.
requirements: Teacher training in cooperative learning strategies and program management, provided via the two-day session described in the report
constraints: Implemented in the reviewed studies with grades 2–6 students in US elementary schools
target_learners: upper elementary and middle-grade students in mixed-ability classrooms
examples: The program description states that within cooperative teams of four, students work to understand the main idea of a story and work through linked writing activities, with rewards based on team performance
key_sources: Cooperative Integrated Reading and Composition®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report, Adolescent Literacy. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/111

article_title: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies — English Language Learners (Reading)
citation: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals
title: PALS three-strategy reciprocal tutoring routine: partner reading and retelling, paragraph shrinking, and prediction relay
description: A recurring lesson-level structure in which paired students alternate tutor and tutee roles across three timed activities. During "partner reading and retelling, the stronger reader reads for five minutes, while the weaker reader serves as the coach by identifying errors, initiating correction procedures, and awarding points". In paragraph shrinking, readers generate main idea statements in 10 words or less for one point per correct response; in prediction relay, the reader predicts before reading half a page and evaluates the prediction afterward. Roles switch after each timed segment.
requirements: Teacher-ranked student pairs formed to decrease reading-ability disparity
Timed segments of approximately five minutes per role, with students switching roles
A correction procedure the tutor uses to help the reader amend inaccurate main idea statements
constraints: In paragraph shrinking, the second reader does not read the same material as the first reader
target_learners: Elementary students in pairs of stronger and weaker readers, including English language learners
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency, sequencing information, generating main idea statements, and generating and evaluating predictions
examples: During prediction relay, the stronger reader has two minutes to predict before reading half a page, reads for five minutes, then has two minutes to evaluate the prediction before students switch roles
key_sources: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. (2010). WWC Intervention Report. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals

article_title: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies — Adolescent Literacy
citation: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Adolescent Literacy — Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/
title: Structured reciprocal peer-tutoring lesson routine with rotating roles and timed activity blocks
description: A repeatable lesson-level design in which student pairs cycle through three timed activities — partner reading, paragraph shrinking, and prediction relay — switching tutor and tutee roles at fixed intervals. In prediction relay, "the reader predicts what is likely to happen on the next page, reads aloud from the page, and summarizes the just-read text, with the tutor deciding whether the predictions are accurate. Students switch roles after five-minute blocks." The stronger reader reads first so the weaker reader can preview the passage and review difficult words before re-reading the same text.
requirements: Teachers train students in the routines beforehand, and pairs are assigned so that one student is proficient in an area where the other is deficient
constraints: Student reading materials are not provided; teachers must select appropriate texts, including informational texts for high school students
examples: In the studied implementation, each partner read aloud connected text for 5 minutes (10 minutes total), paragraph summary ran 20 minutes for the first 4 weeks and was then halved to make room for prediction relay
key_sources: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. (2012). WWC Intervention Report: Adolescent Literacy — Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. https://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/

article_title: Reading Apprenticeship — Grade 9 Literacy
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Apprenticeship®. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://www.wested.org/ReadingApprenticeship
title: Making reading processes visible through teacher modeling and metacognitive classroom conversation
description: A reusable instructional pattern in which the teacher assumes the role of expert reader, modeling and guiding students' text-based problem solving to build comprehension strategies. By incorporating student/teacher discussions about the process of reading into content-area classes, the approach aims to make the teacher's and students' reading processes and knowledge visible to others in the classroom, help students understand and regulate their own reading processes, and develop strategies for overcoming obstacles while reading. Small-group and full-classroom conversations about the thinking process used while reading are fundamental components.
requirements: Teachers must be prepared to examine their own discipline-specific reading during professional development and to model it for students
constraints: The pattern is designed for content-area classes in middle school, high school, and community college settings
target_learners: adolescent learners in content-area classrooms, including struggling readers and English language learners
target_learning_goals: comprehension strategies, self-regulation of reading processes, and overcoming obstacles while reading
examples: Reading Apprenticeship® classrooms integrate the pattern through conversations about the thinking processes that students and teachers use as they read
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Apprenticeship®. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://www.wested.org/ReadingApprenticeship

article_title: Read Naturally — Students with Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: Read Naturally®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Read Naturally®. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.readnaturally.com
title: Three-component fluency-building strategy: modeled reading, repeated timed reading, and student-teacher progress monitoring
description: All four Read Naturally® products share a common fluency-building strategy with three components: "modeling of story reading, repeated reading of text for developing oral reading fluency, and systematic monitoring of student progress by teachers and the students themselves." Students listen to and read along with a fluent recording, do 1-minute practice readings toward a speed goal, then complete a teacher-scored pass timing; they graph scores from initial to final readings and across successive stories so both teacher and student track progress.
requirements: Sequenced texts at the student's reading level
audio recordings of fluent readers
teacher time for pass timings
graphing tools for progress monitoring
constraints: Designed as a supplement to core language arts instruction, not a replacement
target_learners: elementary, middle, or high school students
examples: The report describes students choosing a story, recalling what they know about the topic, reading aloud while the teacher identifies missing words, and graphing words read in one minute
key_sources: Read Naturally®. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Read Naturally®. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.readnaturally.com

article_title: Check & Connect
citation: Dropout Prevention intervention report: Check & Connect. (2015). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Sustained monitor-based check-and-connect mentoring pattern
description: The article describes a recurring instructional-design arrangement: a single monitor who functions as the student's mentor and case worker over multiple years. Monitors provide "basic intervention for all students on their caseload, as well as intensive intervention for students as needed" — regular structured discussions about progress plus intensive problem solving, academic support, and family outreach when risk signs increase. The monitor follows students to different schools as needed.
requirements: Monitors record engagement (attendance, academic performance, disciplinary actions) on a daily basis
Monitors had regular interactions with all students on at least a monthly basis in the 1998 study
constraints: In the 1998 study monitors worked 20 hours a week with an average caseload of 25 students
target_learners: secondary students with disabilities at risk of dropout
examples: In the 2005 study, monitors attended an initial orientation workshop, weekly or biweekly staff meetings, and submitted attendance printouts with monitoring sheets for verification
key_sources: Dropout Prevention intervention report: Check & Connect. (2015). What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/78

article_title: Reading Recovery — Grade 1 Beginning Reading
citation: Reading Recovery®. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Beginning Reading. Updated July 2013. http://www.readingrecovery.org
title: Interactive individualized lesson structure combining reading, letter/word work, and story writing
description: Each Reading Recovery lesson follows a recurring structure: "reading familiar or novel stories, manipulating letters and words, and writing and assembling stories." Lessons are "interactive between the teacher and student, with the teacher carefully monitoring each student's reading behavior," and teachers tailor instruction to accommodate each student's needs. This pattern combines text reading, orthographic work, and composing within a single one-on-one session, with continuous teacher observation guiding what each lesson contains.
requirements: A trained teacher who carefully monitors each student's reading behavior and tailors lessons to individual needs
constraints: Implemented as one-on-one pull-out tutoring for first-grade struggling readers, 30 minutes daily over 12–20 weeks
target_learners: First-grade students struggling in reading and writing
examples: Lessons are discontinued when students demonstrate the ability to consistently read at the average level for their grade—between weeks 12 and 20 of the program
key_sources: Reading Recovery®. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report, Beginning Reading. Updated July 2013. http://www.readingrecovery.org

article_title: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies — Students with Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2012). Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/
title: PALS Reading three-activity session structure: Partner Reading/Retelling, Paragraph Shrinking, and Prediction Relay
description: For grades 2–6, each PALS Reading session sequences three structured activities. In Partner Reading/Retelling the stronger reader reads for five minutes while the weaker reader coaches, identifying errors and awarding points, then roles switch. In Paragraph Shrinking students generate main idea statements paragraph by paragraph with tutor correction. In Prediction Relay the reader predicts what will happen in each upcoming half-page segment, then reads and evaluates the prediction. The pattern pairs each student's reading with immediate peer coaching, error correction, and points.
requirements: Student pairs with one stronger and one weaker reader, formed by teacher judgment, with roles alternating within each activity
constraints: Activities are modified for kindergarten, first grade, and high school; the described structure applies to grades 2–6
target_learners: students in grades 2–6, including students with learning disabilities
examples: Saenz et al. (2005) used this structure for 35 minutes three times a week for 15 weeks, with reading selections chosen at the weaker student's reading level and dyads earning points
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2012). Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/

article_title: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies — Students with Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2012). Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/
title: PALS Math two-activity session structure: coach-modeled self-talk questioning followed by practice
description: For grades 2–6, each PALS Math session includes two activities. In Coaching, "the stronger student (the coach) models a series of questions to encourage the weaker student (the player) to internalize a self-talk method for solving computation or concepts/applications problems"; the coach uses helping and explaining strategies to promote understanding and correct errors, and materials prompt when to switch roles. The second activity, Practice, is a 5- to 10-minute activity addressing the skill just practiced plus easier skills at that grade level.
requirements: Teacher-formed pairs designated by teacher judgment or ongoing curriculum-based measurement data, with coach and player roles prompted to switch by the materials
constraints: The described two-activity structure applies to grades 2–6; activities are modified for other grade levels
target_learners: students in grades 2–6, including students with learning disabilities
examples: In the Fuchs et al. (1995) study, PALS Math ran twice weekly for 25- to 30-minute sessions over 23 weeks, with students trained in five 30-minute sessions before the intervention started
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2012). Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies. WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. http://kc.vanderbilt.edu/pals/

article_title: Teach for America (TFA)
citation: Teach For America. (2016). WWC Intervention Report: Teach For America. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.teachforamerica.org
title: TFA summer training institute combining supervised practice teaching, coaching, and coursework
description: The TFA training institute is a 5- to 7-week residential program in which corps members practice teaching in a real classroom under supervision while receiving observation, feedback, and coursework. The report describes how the institute "includes teaching summer school in a real classroom under the supervision of a regular classroom teacher", observation and feedback from TFA instructional coaches, small-group practice and reflection sessions, lesson planning clinics, and coursework in instructional planning, classroom management, diversity, and literacy development.
requirements: A residential training institute with summer school teaching placements, plus follow-up regional orientation of 1-2 weeks covering student achievement goals, lesson planning, data use, and relationship building
constraints: Training varies by region, though the report says it usually includes an induction, the institute, and a regional orientation
target_learners: novice teachers entering high-need public schools
examples: During training, corps members teach summer school typically for at least 2 hours per day and receive one-on-one coaching from TFA staff during their 2-year commitment
key_sources: Teach For America. (2016). WWC Intervention Report: Teach For America. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.teachforamerica.org

article_title: Science Teachers Learning from Lesson Analysis (STeLLA)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, May). Science Teachers Learning through Lesson Analysis (STeLLA®). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Analysis-of-practice videocase-based professional development with school-based study groups
description: STeLLA®'s core design pattern is analysis of practice: teachers learn a lesson analysis process at a summer institute by discussing videos of experienced teachers, then during the school year videorecord themselves teaching and analyze one another's videorecorded lessons and student work in school-based study groups. In the first half of the year teachers analyze videos of one another delivering model lesson plans; in the second half they collaboratively develop their own lesson plans incorporating STeLLA® teaching strategies and anticipating student misconceptions, then deliver, videorecord, and analyze these lessons.
requirements: A STeLLA® professional development leader works with school-based study groups
Monthly discussion sessions each lasting 3 to 4 hours during the school year
constraints: Study group meetings take place at participating schools, with the professional development leader joining online or on-site depending on availability of local leaders
target_learners: Elementary teachers of science in grades 4 and 5 (in the studied implementation)
target_learning_goals: Learning to convey science content to students
Implementing STeLLA® teaching strategies in teachers' own classrooms
examples: Teachers receive transcripts of program-developed videorecorded lessons and related examples of student work, and BSCS provides online access to videorecordings made by members of their local study group
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, May). Science Teachers Learning through Lesson Analysis (STeLLA®). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/716

article_title: Dual Language Programs
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Dual language programs. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Three-component implementation pattern for dual language programs
description: Table 2 of the report describes three components of dual language program implementation: program leadership and support (a school leadership team of teachers and administrative staff overseeing model selection, development, and evaluation, with district or state training and funding); hiring and training linguistically and culturally competent teachers in both languages; and aligned curriculum, assessments, and instruction in both languages, including a scope and sequence aligned across subjects and grades in both languages.
requirements: Schools establish a school leadership team consisting of teachers and administrative staff responsible for selecting, advocating for, and overseeing the program model.

Teachers must be trained on how students develop bilingualism and biliteracy and, especially for two-way programs, learn how to incorporate student cultural and linguistic backgrounds into instruction.
Schools develop or adopt a scope and sequence and ensure alignment of the curriculum across subjects and grades in both languages.
constraints: Neither study provides specific information about the implementation of the school leadership team, and one study does not provide information on how the schools were supported.
target_learners: elementary and middle school students in one-way and two-way dual language programs
target_learning_goals: academic language development across content areas
examples: In one study the state developed a curriculum aligned with the Common Core standards designed to promote literacy in both languages, plus lesson plans and translated content curricula for math, social sciences, and science.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023, December). Dual language programs. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/726

article_title: Fraction Face-Off!
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Four-activity lesson structure combining explicit instruction, fluency games, and individual practice
description: Each Fraction Face-Off! lesson follows a fixed four-activity structure: "a warm-up word problem, group work during which the teacher demonstrates fraction concepts using explicit instruction, a speed game to build fluency, and a worksheet activity that students complete individually to check their understanding of the fraction concepts." The program pairs frequent fluency practice using speed tests or flashcards with conceptual practice requiring students to explain their reasoning about fractions to the group, plus ongoing assessment through daily worksheets and a cumulative review.
requirements: Up to a week of training for teachers before delivering content, with 1-hour follow-up meetings every other week
constraints: Lessons varied in length between 30 and 35 minutes in the study, and in years 2 through 5 only 25 minutes of each session were the same across the two intervention conditions
target_learners: fourth-grade students who need assistance solving fraction problems
examples: In year 1, each lesson included introduction of concepts or skills (8-12 minutes), group work (8-12 minutes), the speed game (1 minute), and individual work (8 minutes)
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/702

article_title: Fraction Face-Off!
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Deliver supplemental fraction tutoring in small groups three times weekly for 12 weeks
description: The developer recommends "students use Fraction Face-Off! three times a week for 12 weeks for about 30 minutes per session." This dosage was the schedule under which the program's positive effects were demonstrated: in the contributing study, the intervention was delivered three times per week for 12 weeks between September/October and early February, in small groups at a three-to-one ratio, typically during class time or a pull-out time to supplement the math curriculum.
requirements: Schools must provide classroom space if the intervention is not implemented in the student's regular classroom, and make copies of materials and manipulatives for all participating students
constraints: The recommended dosage is three 30- to 35-minute lessons per week; the study delivered sessions during one of three instructional periods of typically 50, 20, or 45 minutes
target_learners: fourth-grade students who have demonstrated difficulty in mathematics
examples: Within each study class, the intervention was delivered by one teacher to small groups (three-to-one ratio) three times per week for 12 weeks, with each teacher responsible for two to four groups
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/702

article_title: Social Skills Training (Early Childhood, Children with Disabilities)
citation: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Behavioral social skills lesson pattern: instruct, model, practice, reinforce
description: The reviewed interventions share a recurring lesson structure: children are instructed on target behaviors, instructors model the behavior, children practice it with peers, and appropriate behavior is reinforced. In Guglielmo and Tryon (2001), "Instructors modeled the activities for the children using puppets and a short skit. Following this activity, children practiced the sharing skills with their peers," with reinforcement including continuous verbal acknowledgment and tangible rewards. LeBlanc and Matson (1995) similarly modeled with a puppet, had children model with a puppet and then with another child, and reinforced during a play phase.
requirements: Target behaviors must be specified (e.g., sharing, being in a group, greeting, initiating play)
Reinforcement of targeted behaviors during and after practice
constraints: In LeBlanc and Matson (1995), children engaging in inappropriate behavior were prompted toward an opposite positive behavior, with a one-minute time-out if they refused
target_learners: preschool children with disabilities or developmental delays
target_learning_goals: age-appropriate social skills such as sharing, joining a group, greeting, and initiating play
examples: Guglielmo and Tryon (2001) taught children to establish eye contact, tap children on the shoulder to gain attention, and ask to play with others
LeBlanc and Matson (1995) split each session into an approximately 15-minute instruction and modeling phase and an approximately 45-minute reinforced play phase
key_sources: Social Skills Training. (2013). What Works Clearinghouse Intervention Report: Early Childhood Education Interventions for Children with Disabilities. U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/578

article_title: Repeated Reading
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2014). Repeated Reading: WWC Intervention Report, Students with Learning Disabilities. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Repeated reading as a flexible practice with seven variable implementation parameters
description: The report describes repeated reading not as a fixed protocol but as a practice whose implementation teachers can vary along seven parameters. As printed, "Teachers can vary" the criterion for progression to the next passage (minimum number of reads or a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute), the instructional settings (teacher-directed, with same-age or cross-age peers, in groups, independently), the purpose, the materials (narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, student- or class-written text), the modalities (silent with a tape, aloud with a model, choral, to a peer, to oneself), the length of the passage read, and the feedback provided on reading errors.
requirements: A teacher who selects passages and sets a progression criterion such as a minimum reading rate of 85–100 words per minute
constraints: The reviewed evidence covers individual delivery with a teacher in grades 5–12; the report does not rate effectiveness for the other configurations it lists
target_learners: students with learning disabilities in grades 5–12 with inadequate reading fluency
examples: Settings range from teacher-directed one-on-one to work with same-age or cross-age peers, groups, or independent practice
Materials may include narrative texts, expository texts, poems, chants, songs, or text written by the student or class
