article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Require mastery of the current concept before advancing to the next in a sequenced math program
description: Symphony Math sequences mathematical concepts and does not let a student move on until the current concept is mastered. Because the time and practice students need is not uniform, the program lets students spend the time they need to master foundational concepts before progressing.
requirements: A sequenced progression of mathematical concepts with mastery assessment at each step
constraints: Requires allowing non-uniform amounts of time and practice per student
examples: A student does not move to the next concept in the Symphony Math sequence until she has mastered the current concept
key_sources: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/symphony-math/

article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Adaptive pacing that accelerates to locate need then slows until understanding is achieved
description: The program quickly moves students through the conceptual progression to identify their area of need, then slows progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved. This two-phase pacing pattern combines rapid diagnosis with remedial slowdown, and also alerts educators when students show signs of struggle.
requirements: A conceptual progression of skills and ongoing performance monitoring to detect the area of need
target_learners: K-8 students needing individualized math practice
target_learning_goals: Identifying and remediating individual areas of need in mathematics
examples: Once the area of need has been identified, the program slows the progress until the necessary understanding has been achieved
key_sources: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/symphony-math/

article_title: eMINTS
citation: eMINTS (enhancing Missouri's Instructional Networked Teaching Strategies): Program description and evidence summary. (2023). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Build principal leadership and observation capacity alongside teacher professional development when implementing an instructional improvement program
description: eMINTS treats implementation leadership as part of the intervention itself: "The model also has a strong emphasis on helping principals understand and lead the program implementation and carry out teacher observations to support teachers' instructional performance." Professional development is thus directed not only at teachers but at principals and technology coordinators, so school leaders can understand, lead, and monitor the program rather than merely host it.
requirements: Principals receive professional development to understand and lead program implementation
Principals conduct teacher observations to support instructional performance
target_learning_goals: instructional quality through observation and support
examples: Professional development is provided to principals, technology coordinators, and classroom teachers in middle schools.
key_sources: eMINTS (enhancing Missouri's Instructional Networked Teaching Strategies): Program description and evidence summary. (2023). Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Token reward with mapped milestone prizes sustaining engagement across tutoring sessions
description: Pirate Math embeds a motivational routine in its tutoring sessions: students receive gold coins for good work and place them on a treasure map. When they reach a picture of a treasure box, they earn a small prize. This recurring reward cycle structures motivation across the 16-week program.
requirements: A treasure map and small prizes must be available across the 16-week session sequence
target_learners: Third graders in remedial math tutoring
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and effort in tutoring sessions
examples: Students receive gold coins for good work, place them on a treasure map, and earn a small prize on reaching the treasure box picture.
key_sources: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/pirate-math/

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Deliver supplemental math tutoring one-to-one outside ordinary math periods, staffed by teachers or trained paraprofessionals
description: Pirate Math delivers tutoring one-to-one, with tutors who may be teachers or paraprofessionals working with students outside of ordinary math periods. This staffing and scheduling model allows struggling third graders to receive intensive individual support without displacing their regular math instruction.
requirements: Paraprofessionals or certified teachers as tutors, with training provided through AIR
constraints: Requires scheduling sessions outside ordinary math periods, three per week over 16 weeks
target_learning_goals: Math calculations and word problem solving
examples: In the qualifying study, low-achieving students received 48 one-to-one sessions from teachers or paraprofessionals outside ordinary math periods.
key_sources: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/pirate-math/

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Zearn Math
citation: Zearn Math evidence review. (2024). https://zearn.org
title: Pair supplemental digital math programs with dedicated implementation support including professional development, coaching, and dosage monitoring
description: The review indicates that significant positive results occurred where Zearn Math was implemented with "accompanying professional development and coaching support for school leaders", which helps schools "establish dedicated time in the schedule for usage, build effective routines, and use data to ensure students reach the recommended dosage of three digital lessons per week". Support includes regular coach check-ins and motivational strategies such as classroom-based challenges to promote consistent lesson completion.
requirements: Dedicated scheduled time for program usage
Professional development and coaching for school leaders
Data-based progress monitoring toward the recommended dosage
Designated school or district points of contact for onboarding and rostering setup
constraints: The pilot implementation without full implementation support found no significant differences, suggesting support may be a boundary condition for effects.
target_learners: Students in grades K-8 in elementary and middle schools
examples: Treatment schools in the Texas RCT received dedicated implementation support including professional development, coaching, and progress monitoring; the Louisiana study likewise provided dedicated implementation support.
key_sources: Zearn Math evidence review. (2024). https://zearn.org

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: OGAP Math Professional Learning System
citation: OGAP Math program description. (2024). Evidence for Learning. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/ogap-math/
title: OGAP strand-based professional learning structure: cohorts of about 24 educators, four onsite days, and two follow-up coaching days
description: OGAP professional learning is organized by Strand, each aligned to a developmental progression in mathematics: Additive Reasoning (K–2), Multiplicative Reasoning (3–5), Fractional Reasoning (3–6), and Proportional Reasoning (6–8). Each strand is delivered to educator cohorts, often around 24 participants, through four onsite professional learning days, with districts able to space sessions several weeks apart. Two onsite follow-up coaching days, often during PLC time, "support transfer into classroom practice." Multiple strands may run simultaneously under the same structure.
requirements: Cohorts of about 24 educators per OGAP Strand
Four onsite professional learning days per strand
Two onsite follow-up coaching days, often scheduled during PLC time
constraints: Districts may choose consecutive sessions or a split schedule, with flexibility to space the sessions several weeks apart
target_learners: K–8 mathematics teachers participating in OGAP strands
target_learning_goals: Transfer of professional learning into classroom practice
Grade-band mathematical reasoning progressions (additive, multiplicative, fractional, proportional)
examples: Strands are aligned to grade-band progressions such as Multiplicative Reasoning (3–5) and Proportional Reasoning (6–8)
key_sources: OGAP Math program description. (2024). Evidence for Learning. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/ogap-math/

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Graspable Math — From Here to There (FH2T)
citation: From Here to There (FH2T): Program Description and Evaluation Evidence. (2023). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au/the-toolkit/from-here-to-there/
title: Expression-transformation puzzle: match a starting expression to an equivalent target form via valid operations
description: The core design pattern of FH2T is a transformation puzzle: "The program presents a starting expression and a mathematically equivalent target expression. Students manipulate the original expression to match the target form." Because moves must be "mathematically valid operations," students practice algebraic manipulation by direct interaction with notation rather than by answering discrete items. The pattern embeds practice of distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations inside the game's goal structure.
requirements: A starting expression paired with a mathematically equivalent target expression
An interface allowing students to drag and transform expressions using mathematically valid operations
constraints: Applied in the article to algebraic expressions and equation solving for introductory prealgebra/algebra
target_learners: Middle and high school students learning introductory prealgebra or algebra
target_learning_goals: Fluency with algebraic manipulation operations, including distribution, factoring, inverse operations, and order of operations
examples: FH2T tasks ask students to transform a given expression into a target form using operations such as distribution and factoring.
key_sources: From Here to There (FH2T): Program Description and Evaluation Evidence. (2023). https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au/the-toolkit/from-here-to-there/

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: My Math Academy
citation: My Math Academy evidence summary. (2022). Age of Learning. https://www.ageoflearning.com/schools/systemcheck/
title: Adaptive game-based design combining scaffolding, embedded assessment, and narrative engagement
description: The program's design pattern combines a math curriculum with adaptive game-based learning: each game activity maps to a learning objective with "an interactive instruction level, as well as several layers of scaffolding and feedback." Adaptivity operates within games, between games, and across the system to give "a customized pathway between skills based on prior performance," with cohesive narrative and interactive characters supporting engagement.
requirements: Device compatibility with the program's minimum technical requirements
constraints: Designed for pre-kindergarten through second grade number sense and operations content
target_learners: Young children in pre-K through 2nd grade
examples: Game-based pretests and final assessment tasks at a granular skill level are embedded throughout the play experience
key_sources: My Math Academy evidence summary. (2022). Age of Learning. https://www.ageoflearning.com/schools/systemcheck/

article_title: SIPPS (Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words)
citation: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Three-level developmental progression of word-recognition instruction with an older-student variant
description: The curriculum organizes word-recognition instruction into "three developmental levels of progression in word recognition: simple alphabetic (SIPPS Beginning Level), spelling-pattern (SIPPS Extension Level), and polysyllabic/morphemic (SIPPS Challenge Level)." A separate variant, SIPPS Plus, covers the simple alphabetic and spelling-pattern phases but is designed specifically for older students in grades 4–12, allowing the same progression to serve adolescent struggling readers.
requirements: Placement testing to locate students at their points of need within a level and lesson
target_learners: K-12 students needing foundational word-recognition instruction
target_learning_goals: Progression from simple alphabetic to spelling-pattern to polysyllabic/morphemic word recognition
examples: SIPPS Plus addresses the simple alphabetic and spelling-pattern phases for students in grades 4-12
key_sources: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/

article_title: SIPPS (Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words)
citation: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Use placement and embedded mastery tests to drive grouping, pacing, and reteaching decisions
description: The article describes an assessment system in which "Assessment data determines placement in the program" and flexible groups based on placement results provide differentiated instruction. Criterion-referenced mastery tests embedded at designated intervals document mastery of phonics and high-frequency words and "support instructional decisions to guide reteaching, which may include adjusting pacing and delivery." This keeps instruction matched to individual progress through an accelerative scope and sequence.
requirements: Initial and ongoing assessment; criterion-referenced mastery tests embedded at designated intervals in each level's scope and sequence
target_learners: K-12 students in differentiated small groups within a foundational reading program
target_learning_goals: Efficient progression through foundational reading skills matched to individual need
examples: Students in the evaluation were placed at points of need within a level and lesson, with progress monitoring used throughout
key_sources: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/

article_title: Expository Reading and Writing Course (ERWC)
citation: Expository Reading and Writing Course (ERWC). (2015). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Expository+Reading+and+Writing+Course
title: ERWC instructional focus on discussion, critical thinking, oral language, genre writing, and rhetorical analysis
description: The ERWC's design centers English instruction on a set of interrelated practices: "discussions of text meaning, developing critical thinking skills, encouraging group discussions, developing oral language skills, developing writing skills in multiple genres, and analyzing the rhetorical features of texts and applying them in student writing." These foci operate across the whole twelfth-grade English course.
requirements: Teachers deliver the ERWC curriculum materials with professional learning and coaching support.
examples: The course replaces ordinary twelfth-grade English classes and applies these foci throughout the year.
key_sources: Expository Reading and Writing Course (ERWC). (2015). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Expository+Reading+and+Writing+Course

article_title: Lexia English Language Development
citation: Lexia English Language Development. (2022). Evidence rating summary. https://www.lexialearning.com
title: Blended online practice with speech-recognition feedback plus teacher-led small-group oral language instruction
description: The program's instructional design combines interactive, student-directed online lessons, in which "speech recognition to provide immediate feedback" supports listening and speaking practice in academic contexts, with teacher-led instruction on oral language, grammar, and vocabulary. Content is organized across 19 content-based levels spanning subjects such as science, math, and social studies, and teachers receive real-time progress data with aligned small-group lesson plans.
requirements: Technology supporting speech recognition and real-time progress reporting
Teachers review performance data and deliver small-group lessons
constraints: Designed as a supplement to core instruction, not a replacement
examples: Students practiced listening and speaking in academic contexts across 19 content-based levels during ELD, literacy, or intervention blocks
key_sources: Lexia English Language Development. (2022). Evidence rating summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/lexia-english/

article_title: Reading Go! (Formerly Reading Rescue)
citation: Reading Go! (formerly Reading Rescue). (2021). Evidence for ESSA program description (no publication date printed on page). https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Daily assessment-driven one-on-one tutoring session with targeted, multisensory literacy components
description: Each daily 30-minute one-on-one session provides a balanced literacy block including fluency building, daily assessments, phonological awareness and word study, sentence writing, and vocabulary development. "Program components are targeted at individual student needs," and tutors "use daily assessments to inform daily instruction within a sequential framework." Components are also multisensory, "incorporating visual, auditory, kinesthetic and tactile teaching methods."
requirements: Trained tutors who administer daily assessments and adjust instruction accordingly
Leveled book sets, tutoring supplies, and training manuals provided by the program
constraints: Delivered in 30-minute daily one-on-one sessions, typically for one semester
examples: Tutors used daily assessments to inform daily instruction within a sequential framework during the studied New York City implementation

article_title: Early Steps
citation: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Daily one-to-one tutoring session structure: re-reading, word study, sentence writing, new books
description: Early Steps sessions follow a repeating daily structure in which tutors use "a series of leveled, non-phonetic books" and "follow a daily schedule of re-reading familiar books, systematic word study, sentence writing, and introducing new books." This 30-minute, five-days-a-week structure recurs across the entire first grade year, giving each session a predictable sequence of familiar reading, word-level work, writing, and new text introduction.
requirements: One-to-one delivery in 30-minute sessions five days a week over the entire first grade year
trained tutors
target_learning_goals: beginning reading skills including word attack and comprehension
examples: Tutors deliver the schedule daily across the first grade year in the evaluated urban Tennessee schools

article_title: Early Steps
citation: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Staff one-to-one tutoring with trained school staff rather than community volunteers
description: The program specifies that "Classroom teachers, reading teachers, or well-prepared paraprofessionals are needed to serve as tutors," while "Community volunteers are not suggested as tutors." Tutoring quality is treated as depending on staff who receive extensive training, observation, and feedback, so schools implementing one-to-one tutoring should assign trained staff rather than volunteers.
requirements: Access to classroom teachers, reading teachers, or well-prepared paraprofessionals to serve as tutors
constraints: Community volunteers are not suggested as tutors
target_learning_goals: improved word attack and passage comprehension
examples: In the evaluated model, tutors may be the child's own teacher, a Title I teacher, or a part-time teacher added to the staff
key_sources: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/early-steps/

article_title: CAPIT Reading
citation: CAPIT Reading: Evidence Rating (Moderate). (2024). https://www.capitlearning.com/
title: Assessment-based placement with self-paced, competency-based progression
description: The program places each student at an appropriate starting level via an initial assessment and then lets students advance individually. "Students begin with an assessment that places them at the appropriate level, allowing them to progress through the program at their own pace." The competency-based digital platform delivers "individualized instruction and immediate feedback" so progression depends on demonstrated competency rather than fixed pacing.
requirements: An initial placement assessment
A competency-based digital platform providing individualized instruction and immediate feedback
constraints: Evaluated in pre-kindergarten classrooms as a supplemental program
target_learners: PK-3 students across all three tiers of instruction
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills, closing reading gaps
examples: In the Florida matched comparison study, pre-kindergarten students progressed through the program at their own pace after assessment-based placement.

article_title: i-Ready Classroom Mathematics
citation: i-Ready Classroom Mathematics. (2024). Curriculum Associates. https://www.curriculumassociates.com/professional-development
title: Lessons grounded in NCTM Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices emphasizing discourse, reasoning, and real-world connections
description: iRCL lessons are designed around the Effective Mathematics Teaching Practices from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics. The page states lessons "emphasize discourse, reasoning, and real-world connections," and the program is closely aligned with grade-level standards and designed to support all learners, including those needing additional scaffolding.
requirements: Alignment with grade-level standards; print and digital materials including teacher guides and manipulatives
target_learners: K-8 mathematics students, including those who need additional scaffolding
examples: The program combines print and digital materials, including teacher guides, student workbooks, practice tools, and hands-on manipulatives
key_sources: i-Ready Classroom Mathematics. (2024). Curriculum Associates. https://www.curriculumassociates.com/professional-development

article_title: Core-Plus Mathematics Project
citation: Core-Plus Mathematics evidence review. (2019). https://www.coreplusmath.org
title: Provide teachers multi-day professional development before and during Core-Plus implementation
description: The review specifies professional development as an implementation requirement for Core-Plus Mathematics: ideally a 5-day summer workshop prior to implementation and at least 2 PD days during the first year. In the qualifying studies, teachers received up to a total of two weeks of professional development before school opening and periodically during the school year to develop understanding of the curriculum organization, content progressions, and associated instructional and assessment strategies.
requirements: Ideally a 5-day summer workshop prior to implementation and at least 2 PD days during the first year
target_learners: High school mathematics teachers implementing Core-Plus Mathematics
target_learning_goals: Understanding of the curriculum organization, content progressions, and associated instructional and assessment strategies
examples: Teachers in the qualifying studies received up to a total of two weeks of professional development before school opening and periodically during the school year

article_title: Catapult Learning's Educational Services
citation: Catapult Learning's Wraparound Supplemental Educational Services. (2024). Evidence review, program description and outcomes. https://www.catapultlearning.com
title: Deliver supplemental academic services in a structured environment with a low student-to-teacher ratio
description: The Wraparound program is delivered in a structured environment with a low student-to-teacher ratio, which the page presents as part of how the program aims to accelerate academic achievement while fostering a supportive learning atmosphere. Staffing criteria by service type (certified instructors, certified counselors, experienced coaches) support this delivery model.
requirements: Instructors with state-compliant certification; counselors with certification and/or MSW; coaches with 2 years of K-8 experience
constraints: No required technology component to the program model or the delivery of services
target_learners: K-12 students receiving supplemental educational services
target_learning_goals: Accelerated academic achievement in literacy and math
examples: The evaluated program model paired small-group AchieveMath and AchieveLiteracy instruction with counseling and special education support in a parochial school district

article_title: Reading Edge
citation: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/
title: Team-based cooperative reading with team recognition based on average member scores
description: The program organizes reading instruction around small cooperative teams whose members prepare one another for individual assessments. "Teams are recognized based on the average of all members' scores on these assessments," which makes each student's preparation valuable to teammates. This recognition structure pairs cooperative practice with individually administered assessments rather than group products.
requirements: 4-5 member teams
individual assessments of reading skills
a recognition mechanism tied to team average scores
target_learning_goals: reading skills built through peer support and individual accountability
examples: Students engage in partner reading, story retelling, story-related writing, word mastery, and story-structure activities to prepare themselves and their teammates for individual assessments.

article_title: Reading Edge
citation: The Reading Edge. (2008). https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/the-reading-edge/
title: Teach metacognitive reading skills explicitly within cooperative team reading instruction
description: Within the Reading Edge approach, cooperative team activities are paired with direct instruction in self-regulatory reading strategies: "Instruction focuses on explicit teaching of metacognitive skills, such as clarification, summarization, predication, and graphic organizers." The principle is that peer team structures and explicit strategy teaching operate together, with teams using these strategies as they prepare for assessments.
requirements: team structures in which students prepare themselves and teammates for individual assessments
explicit lessons on clarification, summarization, predication, and graphic organizers
examples: Reading Edge students engage in partner reading, story retelling, story-related writing, word mastery, and story-structure activities alongside explicit metacognitive instruction.

article_title: Lectura Proactiva/ Intervenciones tempranas de la lectura
citation: Lectura Proactiva (Intervenciones tempranas de la lectura) — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program summary, no author line printed. https://www.evidenceforesight.org/
title: Deliver Lectura Proactiva with extensive professional development and coaching, since the same level of PD is essential to expect positive outcomes
description: The article states that in its successful evaluations the intervention was delivered by bilingual certified teachers who “received extensive professional development and coaching from the developers,” specifically 18 hours of professional development plus frequent staff development sessions and coaching. It concludes that “The same level of PD is essential to expect positive outcomes,” making implementation fidelity through training a condition of effectiveness.

18 hours of professional development plus frequent staff development sessions and coaching from the developers
constraints: Positive outcomes should not be expected without the same level of professional development
target_learners: Spanish-speaking early readers in elementary grades
target_learning_goals: Accelerating the transition to reading in English
examples: In the research schools, intervention teachers received 18 hours of professional development, in addition to frequent staff development sessions and coaching.

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Reduce math concepts to small steps to mastery, then build back up incrementally
description: In JUMP Math, "Math concepts are reduced to increasingly smaller steps until students achieve mastery, then built back up incrementally to meet the curriculum demands." Students receive extensive practice at each step. This stepwise reduction-and-rebuild structure is the core instructional mechanism of the program's guided-discovery approach.
requirements: Extensive practice at each step before moving on
target_learning_goals: mastering math concepts and meeting curriculum demands
examples: The program's teachers guides move students towards discovering target concepts through the sequence of small steps.

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Use ongoing assessment to ensure comprehension before moving to new material
description: JUMP Math treats assessment as continuous: "Assessment is ongoing and considered essential to ensure comprehension before moving on to new material." This gates progression on demonstrated understanding rather than fixed pacing, complementing the program's stepwise mastery structure and individual pacing within a shared class concept.
requirements: Ongoing assessment embedded in the lesson sequence
target_learning_goals: comprehension of math concepts before progression
examples: Students do easier or more challenging work, or gain more practice, relating to the lesson concept until they are ready to move on.
key_sources: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/jump-math/

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Use concrete models strategically and remove them as soon as students can work without them
description: JUMP Math uses "a range of models (concrete materials, tables, diagrams) ... strategically to help students grasp abstract concepts but the models are removed as soon as students are able to work without these supports." The principle is deliberate, temporary scaffolding: models support abstraction but are faded promptly rather than retained.
requirements: Concrete materials, tables, or diagrams available to support abstract concepts
examples: The program's practice of removing models as soon as students can work without supports.

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Streamline student materials and reserve lesson detail for teacher guides to protect working memory
description: JUMP Math has no student textbooks; students complete work in "practice and assessment guides that are streamlined to limit extraneous information and contain only the essential language." Lesson details are reserved for teachers' guides "so that teachers can control the timing and amount of information the students receive so as not to overwhelm student working memory."
requirements: Detailed teachers guides separate from streamlined student guides
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous load while learning math concepts
examples: Smart board materials are not required but many teachers choose to use them.

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS) — Reading

Peer interaction is structured by "a simple error correction strategy with each other, under guidance of a teacher", keeping correction in students' hands while the teacher oversees. The pattern spans phonemic awareness through story retelling.

On-site coaches needed

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI)
citation: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org
title: Align Tier 2 supplemental reading instruction with Tier 1 core instruction through teacher professional development and materials
description: The program's central design principle is alignment: it provides "teachers with professional development and materials to improve the alignment of Tier 2 with Tier 1 core instruction." Core reading teachers also receive professional days on the same strategies, so both tiers teach the same content with shared routines.

Professional development workbooks and a Leadership Guide
target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills, vocabulary, and comprehension aligned with the Common Core State Standards

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction (ECRI)
citation: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org
title: Tiered reading delivery pattern: 90 minutes whole-group core plus 30 minutes small-group Tier 2 for all struggling readers
description: The studied program used a tiered time structure: "all students, experimental and control, received 90 minutes of core reading instruction and 30 minutes of Tier 2 (supplemental) instruction." Core instruction is whole group with classroom teachers; intervention occurs in small groups of 3-5 students led by teachers or instructional assistants.
requirements: Classroom teachers deliver whole-group core instruction
Teachers or instructional assistants deliver small-group Tier 2 intervention
constraints: The program does not require technology
target_learners: first grade students, including struggling readers
target_learning_goals: foundational reading skills delivered through aligned core and supplemental instruction
examples: In the Oregon and Massachusetts study, both experimental and control students received the same 90-minute core block and 30-minute Tier 2 block.
key_sources: Enhanced Core Reading Instruction. (2017). Evidence review summary. https://www.evidenceforesight.org

article_title: PAX Good Behavior Game — Math
citation: PAX Good Behavior Game. (2021). Evidence Rating. https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/pax-good-behavior-game/
title: Team-based group contingency with checkmarks and small privileges to encourage peer support for appropriate behavior
description: The pattern divides students into two or more teams and applies a group contingency: when a team member violates class rules, the team receives a checkmark on the whiteboard, and the team with the fewest checkmarks, or all teams meeting a criterion, receives a small privilege such as lining up first for recess. The summary states "This group contingency is intended to create a situation in which students encourage and assist their peers to behave appropriately."
requirements: Class rules must be discussed and agreed upon by the students themselves
Teacher monitoring of student behavior during lessons
constraints: Privileges are small, such as the opportunity to line up first for recess
target_learning_goals: self- and peer-regulation of classroom behavior
examples: Teams receive checkmarks on the whiteboard for rule violations; the winning team or all teams meeting criterion line up first for recess.
key_sources: PAX Good Behavior Game. (2021). Evidence Rating. https://www.evidencebasedprograms.org/programs/pax-good-behavior-game/

article_title: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs — Family Engagement
citation: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs™. (2025). Evidence review summary. https://www.justrightreader.com
title: Personalized, relevant decodable texts with named students and meaningful storylines to foster ownership and reading identity
description: Each pack is personalized with the student's name and includes books featuring relevant characters and meaningful storylines, along with writing pages that strengthen the connection between reading and writing. The article states "This personalized and relevant design fosters ownership, increases engagement and confidence, and supports the development of strong reading identities."
requirements: Books must be matched to each student's phonics skill level and personalized with the student's name.
examples: Packs include writing pages that connect reading and writing practice.
key_sources: Just Right Reader Take-Everywhere Literacy Packs™. (2025). Evidence review summary. https://www.justrightreader.com

article_title: Thinking Math! by Innovamat
citation: Thinking Math! (Innovamat core curriculum) evidence rating summary. (2025). https://www.innovamat.com
title: Curriculum design combining learning progressions, CPA model, and spaced/interleaved practice
description: The curriculum is "built around research-based learning progressions, a Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract model, and rich mathematical activities designed to connect concepts, interleave and space practice for long-term retention, and provide meaningful contexts for learning." This design pattern organizes content sequencing, activity design, and practice scheduling across the PreK-8 program.
requirements: Teacher lesson guides and manipulative materials to enact the progression-based, CPA-aligned activities
examples: Rich mathematical activities interleave and space practice for long-term retention and provide meaningful contexts for learning
key_sources: Thinking Math! (Innovamat core curriculum) evidence rating summary. (2025). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/innovamat-2/

article_title: Parent Teacher Home Visits
citation: Academic Performance — Parent Teacher Home Visits. (2021). Evidence summary. https://www.evidenceforesscp.org
title: Two-visit home visit structure: relationship-building first, academics second
description: PTHV organizes home visits as a two-visit sequence embedded in ongoing communication. The first visit is relationship-building and occurs in the summer or early fall; a second visit later focuses on academics or another relevant issue for the student or family. The page describes it as "a two-visit model, PTHV encourages the first relationship-building visit to occur in the summer or early fall, followed by ongoing communication throughout the year."
requirements: Visits are voluntary and arranged in advance
Teachers are trained and compensated for visits
target_learning_goals: Building teacher-family relationships and improving instruction for the learner
examples: Educators listen, ask questions, and make observations during visits that they take back to their classrooms to improve instruction.
key_sources: Academic Performance — Parent Teacher Home Visits. (2021). Evidence summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/parent-teacher-home-visits/

article_title: Connect Science
citation: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://www.connectscience.org
title: Service-learning integrated elementary science unit pattern combining NGSS practices, collaborative skills, and a service project
description: This pattern organizes an elementary science unit around three integrated strands: standards-aligned science instruction, explicit social and collaborative skills teaching, and a facilitated service-learning experience. The article describes Connect Science as designed "to prepare teachers to use Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) instructional practices, teach social and collaborative skills, and facilitate a service-learning experience in their science class." The sequence of 31 lessons runs 14 weeks or more and can be integrated with other content instruction.
requirements: Teacher professional development prior to implementation
science materials kit and trade books accompanying the lessons
constraints: Designed for fourth grade; lessons replace existing science units
examples: The evaluation implemented the pattern as 30 lessons of 30-50 minutes each over 14-22 weeks, compared against business-as-usual science instruction.
key_sources: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/connect-science/

article_title: Connect Science
citation: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://www.connectscience.org
title: Adopt Connect Science without additional staffing, using existing classroom teachers trained through its professional development
description: The program is designed to be delivered by regular classroom teachers rather than added personnel: the article states "No additional staffing requirements." Implementation instead depends on teacher preparation through the staged professional development sequence and provision of a manual, science materials kit, and trade books, making adoption a matter of teacher training and materials rather than new hires.
requirements: Teachers complete the professional development sequence and receive the lesson manual and materials kit
constraints: Teachers will need computers to access the web for videos, resources etc.
target_learning_goals: science achievement through NGSS-aligned, service-learning instruction
examples: In the cluster randomized evaluation, treatment classroom teachers delivered the lessons after summer professional development, with no additional staff reported.
key_sources: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/connect-science/

article_title: Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Five implementation challenges of delivering LLI in secondary schools
description: The Oakland evaluation enumerates five challenges schools faced implementing LLI at the secondary level: "delayed start dates and varying end dates", "tradeoffs between pullout groups and scheduled classes", "skipped and modified lesson components", "limited teacher training", and "students’ attendance and engagement at the high school level". This enumerated list characterizes how a packaged elementary-grade intervention translates imperfectly to secondary scheduling and engagement contexts.
requirements: Schools must schedule LLI sessions without displacing grade-level classes and must train teachers in the program.
constraints: Challenges were documented in Oakland secondary schools; the brief does not claim they generalize to elementary settings.
target_learners: Secondary students reading multiple years below grade level
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and English language arts/literacy standards mastery
examples: In Oakland, schools delayed starts, varied end dates, traded off pullout groups against scheduled classes, skipped or modified lesson components, provided limited teacher training, and struggled with high-school attendance and engagement.
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Leveled Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: Results from a Randomized Controlled Trial in Oakland Schools. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/leveled-literacy-intervention-for-secondary-students-results-from-a-randomized-controlled-trial

article_title: Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools
citation: Agodini, R., Harris, B., Atkins-Burnett, S., Heaviside, S., Novak, T., & Murphy, R. (2009). Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/achievement-effects-of-four-early-elementary-school-math-curricula-findings-from-first-graders-in-39-schools
title: Choose early elementary math curricula based on rigorous experimental evidence of achievement effects, since textbook-based programs differ in impact
description: The report addresses a long-standing debate among educators and policymakers over "which textbooks and their associated instructional approaches have the greatest impact on student learning in key subjects." Its experimental evidence shows measurable achievement differences among four widely used first-grade math curricula, supporting curriculum selection informed by rigorous comparative effectiveness evidence rather than by adoption defaults.
requirements: Comparative experimental evidence of the kind produced by the federal evaluation, in which schools are assigned to curricula and achievement outcomes are compared.
constraints: The evidence reported here covers first graders in 39 schools in the 2006-2007 cohort; effects for other grades and later cohorts are not reported on this page.
examples: Mathematica's large-scale federal study assigned 39 first-grade schools to four math programs and found significantly higher achievement under Math Expressions and Saxon Math.
key_sources: Agodini, R., Harris, B., Atkins-Burnett, S., Heaviside, S., Novak, T., & Murphy, R. (2009). Achievement Effects of Four Early Elementary School Math Curricula: Findings from First Graders in 39 Schools. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/achievement-effects-of-four-early-elementary-school-math-curricula-findings-from-first-graders-in-39-schools

article_title: Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes
citation: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes
title: Three-domain organization of middle grades math outcome measures
description: The menu organizes measurement of middle grades math outcomes into three domains: students' "math skills and knowledge", "math perceptions and beliefs", and "math use beyond the classroom". This taxonomy lets educators, district leaders, researchers, and funders select measures spanning performance, dispositions, and out-of-school engagement rather than achievement alone.
requirements: Users select measures matched to the domain of the outcome they intend to measure
examples: The resource's summary lists the three domains as the scope of its curated measures
key_sources: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes

article_title: Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes
citation: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes
title: Assess measure quality with explicit criteria plus context-fit questions before adopting a measure
description: When choosing a measure of student outcomes, apply a set of quality criteria and then ask context-specific questions to judge fit. The resource "includes a set of criteria that can be used to assess measure quality, as well as context-specific questions to help readers determine if a specific measure is a good fit for their unique circumstances." Quality and fit are treated as distinct checks.
requirements: A defined set of measure-quality criteria
Context-specific questions about the adopting setting
constraints: Fit judgments depend on the reader's unique circumstances, so criteria alone do not guarantee fit
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable measurement of math outcomes
examples: The menu pairs its curated measure list with quality criteria and context-specific fit questions for educators, district leaders, researchers, and funders
key_sources: Julie Bruch, Jasmine Forde, Ijun Lai, Veronica Sotelo Muñoz. (2022). Menu of Measures: High-Quality Measures of Middle Years Math Student Outcomes. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/menu-of-measures-high-quality-measures-of-middle-years-math-student-outcomes

article_title: Examining Student and Teacher Math Learning: Lessons from Three Summer Programs
citation: Gregory Chojnacki, Kate Place, Kara Conroy. (2023). Examining Student and Teacher Math Learning: Lessons from Three Summer Programs. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/examining-student-and-teacher-math-learning-lessons-from-three-summer-programs
title: Design summer math programs with attention to teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment
description: The brief reports that "The three summer programs identified lessons on teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment that would improve future implementation." Findings are intended to "inform school districts on the implementation of summer programs" and to "highlight lessons for program providers seeking to refine their programs."
requirements: Program implementers should attend to teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment.
target_learners: grade 6-8 students in summer math programs
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of summer math learning programs
examples: The three evaluated programs generated implementation lessons in teacher training, program monitoring, and student recruitment for future rounds.
key_sources: Gregory Chojnacki, Kate Place, Kara Conroy. (2023). Examining Student and Teacher Math Learning: Lessons from Three Summer Programs. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/examining-student-and-teacher-math-learning-lessons-from-three-summer-programs

article_title: Sustaining Effective Teacher Practice: The Impact of the EL Education Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Development on Teachers' Instruction
citation: Jane Choi, Scott Richman, Sarah Dolfin. (2018). Sustaining Effective Teacher Practice: The Impact of the EL Education Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Development on Teachers' Instruction. Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Pair a standards-aligned curriculum with intensive professional development to build lasting teacher practice
description: The article presents combining a standards-aligned curriculum with intensive professional development as a way "to address the need for high quality and lasting professional learning for teachers". EL Education developed the Teacher Potential Project, which "includes a Common Core State Standards (CCSS)-aligned EL Education Language Arts Curriculum in combination with intensive PD", and an independent evaluation found a significantly greater proportion of TPP teachers demonstrated and sustained CCSS-aligned instructional practices compared with teachers receiving district-provided curriculum and PD.
requirements: A standards-aligned curriculum combined with intensive, sustained professional development for participating teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained CCSS-aligned instructional practices, including promoting higher-order thinking and text-based evidence use
examples: EL Education developed the Teacher Potential Project combining its CCSS-aligned Language Arts Curriculum with intensive PD; Mathematica's independent i3-funded study found significantly more TPP teachers demonstrated and sustained CCSS-aligned practices than district-supported comparison teachers.
key_sources: Jane Choi, Scott Richman, Sarah Dolfin. (2018). Sustaining Effective Teacher Practice: The Impact of the EL Education Language Arts Curriculum and Professional Development on Teachers' Instruction. Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sustaining-effective-teacher-practice-the-impact-of-the-el-education-language-arts-curriculum

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Develop a culture of data use among all levels of district staff
description: The brief's first key recommendation is that districts should "Develop a culture of data use among all levels of staff." It frames effective data use as an organizational capacity issue rather than a purely technical one, arguing that strategic use of data to inform education policy and improve instruction depends on staff at every level engaging with data. The recommendation is one of four the brief offers to districts building data-use capacity.
requirements: Districts must have essential data systems and supports in place before strategic use challenges can be addressed
target_learning_goals: strategic use of data to inform education policy and improve instruction
examples: The brief draws data and supporting examples from work conducted as part of the evaluation of strategic data use initiatives
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Ask the right questions and use data aligned with district goals
description: The brief's second key recommendation is to "Ask the right questions and use the correct data to support district goals." It observes that many districts do not know what questions to ask or what data to use, so question formulation and data selection are treated as capacities districts must deliberately develop. The recommendation ties data analysis directly to district improvement goals.
requirements: Districts need clarity on their goals so that questions and data selection can support them
target_learning_goals: formulating answerable questions and selecting appropriate data to support district goals
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation, drawing examples from the strategic data use initiative evaluation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Correctly interpret data findings to improve policy and practice
description: The brief's third key recommendation is to "Correctly interpret findings to improve policy and practice." It notes that many districts do not know how to interpret findings, positioning interpretation as a distinct capacity from data collection or question formulation. Correct interpretation is presented as the step that connects analysis to actual improvements in policy and instruction.
requirements: Districts need the capacity to interpret analysis findings, not just generate them
target_learning_goals: interpreting data findings to improve policy and instructional practice
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Secure and dedicate resources to conduct analyses and interpret findings
description: The brief's fourth key recommendation is to "Secure and dedicate resources to conduct analyses and interpret findings." It treats analytic and interpretive work as requiring committed resources rather than residual staff effort, making resourcing a precondition for the other recommendations. The recommendation is drawn from the brief's work with districts in strategic data use initiatives.
requirements: Districts must allocate dedicated resources for conducting analyses and interpreting findings
target_learning_goals: building organizational capacity for data analysis and interpretation
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: Scaling Programs with Research Evidence and Effectiveness (SPREE)
citation: Nan Maxwell, Scott Richman. (2019). Scaling Programs with Research Evidence and Effectiveness (SPREE). The Foundation Review, vol. 11, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use the SPREE process to identify and provide the support grantees need to demonstrate effectiveness and build scaling conditions
description: The article recommends that funders use the SPREE process to diagnose what grantees need. It states the process "can also help funders identify and provide the kind of support grantees need in demonstrating that an intervention is effective and in building the conditions needed to scale it successfully." This makes grantee support a deliberate funder activity rather than an afterthought.
requirements: Funders must engage with grantees through the SPREE process to assess their needs for demonstrating effectiveness and scaling
target_learners: Funders and grantee organizations implementing evidence-based interventions
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating intervention effectiveness and building conditions needed for successful scaling
examples: The Corporation for National and Community Service has applied the SPREE process since 2016 to support funded interventions
key_sources: Nan Maxwell, Scott Richman. (2019). Scaling Programs with Research Evidence and Effectiveness (SPREE). The Foundation Review, vol. 11, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/scaling-programs-with-research-evidence-and-effectiveness-spree

article_title: Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial. Working Paper 62. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Schedule adolescent reading interventions so students do not miss grade-level content
description: This principle holds that pull-out intervention arrangements for adolescent struggling readers should be designed so that students do not sacrifice access to grade-level coursework. The Oakland LLI trial found that "Students who were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI were particularly negatively affected, possibly as a result of missing grade-level content." Scheduling is therefore a design lever, not just a logistical detail.
requirements: Intervention scheduling must account for which classes students would otherwise attend
constraints: The article frames the missing-content explanation as possible, not established
target_learners: struggling adolescent readers in secondary grades
target_learning_goals: mastery of grade-level English language arts/literacy standards
examples: In the Oakland trial, some students were pulled out of other classes to receive LLI, and this subgroup showed particularly negative outcomes
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez, Sophie MacIntyre, Pilar Beccar-Varela. (2018). Challenges in Adolescent Reading Intervention: Evidence from a Randomized Control Trial. Working Paper 62. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/challenges-in-adolescent-reading-intervention-evidence-from-a-randomized-control-trial

article_title: Impacts of Blended Learning Tutoring Models on Math Achievement After COVID-19: Results from Saga Education
citation: Laura Meyer, Lily Fesler, Anna Gu, Caroline Lauver. (2024). Impacts of Blended Learning Tutoring Models on Math Achievement After COVID-19: Results from Saga Education. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/impacts-of-blended-learning-tutoring-models-on-math-achievement-after-covid-19
title: Use blended tutoring models that alternate individual online math practice with small-group tutoring when in-person tutor hiring is difficult
description: Saga's blended tutoring models "alternated individual online math practice with student tutoring in small groups provided by an in-person or remote tutor." The report finds online tutoring models "have promise, especially when it is challenging to hire in-person tutors," making this a viable staffing-flexible design for math support.
requirements: Requires tutors available in-person or remotely to lead small-group tutoring sessions alternating with individual online practice
constraints: Impacts were larger in schools with fewer staffing challenges and groups of two students or fewer; attendance showed a small negative impact
target_learners: High school math students in districts recovering from COVID-19 learning disruption
target_learning_goals: Algebra and geometry achievement and math grades
examples: Saga Education implemented high-dosage online, in-person, and hybrid tutoring in three U.S. school districts during the 2021-2022 school year.
key_sources: Laura Meyer, Lily Fesler, Anna Gu, Caroline Lauver. (2024). Impacts of Blended Learning Tutoring Models on Math Achievement After COVID-19: Results from Saga Education. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/impacts-of-blended-learning-tutoring-models-on-math-achievement-after-covid-19

article_title: A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement
citation: Kate Place, Kara Conroy, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Engage the community in focus as collaborators throughout all phases of research and design
description: Evidence-based innovation should begin by identifying a need, problem, or challenge together with the community whose goals should drive design. The publication states that "The M&E approach engages this community as collaborators throughout all phases of research and design," making sustained partnership a core feature rather than a one-time consultation.
requirements: Identify the need, problem, or challenge in partnership with the community in focus before design begins
target_learners: Communities in focus whose goals drive solution design, such as schools and districts
target_learning_goals: Ensuring solution design and evidence building align with community goals
examples: The M&E approach was applied in the evaluation of middle years math teaching and learning solutions prepared for the Gates Foundation
key_sources: Kate Place, Kara Conroy, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-road-map-for-building-evidence-that-drives-learning-and-improvement

article_title: Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers
citation: Hill, C. J., Scher, L., Haimson, J., & Granito, K. (2023). Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Conduct implementation analyses within impact studies so educators can judge local fit
description: The guide's rationale is that implementation analyses conducted as part of impact studies serve adoption decisions: they 'can help educators know whether a tested intervention is likely to be a good fit for their own settings'. Because impacts alone do not reveal what delivery conditions produced them, embedding implementation research gives practitioners the information needed to judge transferability to their contexts.
requirements: Impact studies should incorporate implementation analyses for their findings to inform local adoption decisions.
target_learning_goals: Judge whether an evidence-based intervention fits a local setting
examples: The guide was written to help researchers design and conduct these kinds of analyses within impact studies.
key_sources: Hill, C. J., Scher, L., Haimson, J., & Granito, K. (2023). Conducting Implementation Research in Impact Studies of Education Interventions: A Guide for Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or abandon a solution
description: The checklist's activities focus on iterative learning rather than a one-way march through phases. Teams may complete a phase multiple times, move backwards to a previous phase, or abandon a solution altogether based on what they learn. This principle frames evidence building as a cyclical design process in which findings at any phase can send teams back to earlier design work.
requirements: Teams must be willing to revisit or repeat phases based on evidence gathered
constraints: Iteration may mean abandoning a solution altogether
target_learning_goals: designing and refining solutions through iterative evidence building
examples: The checklist explicitly states that iterative learning may mean completing a phase multiple times or moving backwards to a previous phase
key_sources: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-checklist-design-the-solution-phase-1

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Ground solution design in a well-defined theory of change developed with the priority community
description: Phase 1 of the evidence-building process directs users to develop a solution based on a well-defined theory of change for how that solution is expected to improve outcomes for students or teachers in a priority community. The design work is done in collaboration with stakeholders from that community, so the causal logic connecting the solution to outcomes is explicit before refinement and testing begin.
requirements: A well-defined theory of change must be articulated before the solution proceeds to later phases
constraints: The theory of change is specific to outcomes for students or teachers in the identified priority community
target_learning_goals: articulating how a solution is expected to improve outcomes
examples: The Phase 1 checklist document guides users through developing a solution based on a theory of change in collaboration with community stakeholders
key_sources: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Design the Solution (Phase 1). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-checklist-design-the-solution-phase-1

article_title: Understanding the Capacity of State Apprenticeship Systems: Apprenticeship Evidence-Building Portfolio
citation: Alicia Harrington, Ryan Ruggiero, Samina Sattar, Lauren Eyster. (2022). Understanding the Capacity of State Apprenticeship Systems: Apprenticeship Evidence-Building Portfolio. Urban Institute. https://www.urban.org
title: Eight-characteristic framework of state apprenticeship system capacity
description: The report organizes state apprenticeship system capacity around an enumerated set of characteristics, spanning program registration, employer recruitment, apprentice diversity, rural and opioid-related expansion, financial incentives, costs and federal grants, COVID-19 impacts, and data infrastructure. The report states it covers "variation of systems across states in key characteristics" and lists them as topics for the series. The framework structures both this overview and the later state interviews.

constraints: Applies to United States state-level Registered Apprenticeship systems

examples: The report lists characteristics including "strategies for recruiting employers" and "the role of financial incentives in expanding apprenticeship"

article_title: Comparing the Reliability and Predictive Power of Child, Teacher, and Guardian Reports of Noncognitive Skills
citation: Shuaizhang Feng, Yujie Han, James J. Heckman, Tim Kautz. (2022). Comparing the Reliability and Predictive Power of Child, Teacher, and Guardian Reports of Noncognitive Skills. The Proceedings of the National Academy Sciences, vol. 119, issue 6. https://www.pnas.org
title: Collect teacher reports when a single perspective on children's noncognitive skills must suffice
description: Because collecting ratings from multiple perspectives about a single child is costly and the article finds child and guardian reports add minimal predictive power beyond teacher reports, programs needing one perspective should rely on teacher reports. The article states "teacher reports have the highest internal consistency and are the most predictive of children's later cognitive outcomes and behavior in school." This applies to program evaluation and monitoring school systems.
requirements: A teacher who knows the child must be available to provide the rating.
constraints: Collecting data from multiple perspectives is costly, and the article notes there is limited evidence on the benefits of this approach.
target_learning_goals: measurement of noncognitive or socioemotional skills such as persistence and self-control
examples: The study compared child, guardian, and teacher reports in a longitudinal survey for program evaluation and school-system monitoring purposes.
key_sources: Shuaizhang Feng, Yujie Han, James J. Heckman, Tim Kautz. (2022). Comparing the Reliability and Predictive Power of Child, Teacher, and Guardian Reports of Noncognitive Skills. article_title: Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science
citation: Kautz, T., Milkman, K. L., Gromet, D., et al. as printed in full author line. (2021). Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science. Nature, vol. 600. https://www.nature.com
title: Test many intervention ideas at once in a shared population and outcome to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science
description: The article recommends running many interventions concurrently in the same population on the same objectively measured outcome for the same duration, because typical scattered studies lack comparability. Because "Forecasts by impartial judges failed to predict which interventions would be most effective," the authors argue this "underscor[es] the value of testing many ideas at once and, therefore, the potential for megastudies to improve the evidentiary value of behavioural science."
requirements: A large shared population, an objectively measured outcome held constant across arms, a fixed duration, and multiple independent teams designing interventions.
constraints: In the demonstrated megastudy, only 8% of interventions produced behaviour change significant and measurable after the four-week intervention, so parallel testing does not guarantee durable effects.
target_learners: Adults targeted by applied behavioural-science interventions, here fitness-chain members
target_learning_goals: Identifying which behaviour-change interventions work, e.g. increasing physical exercise
examples: 30 scientists from 15 different US universities worked in small independent teams to design 54 different four-week digital programmes encouraging exercise, all compared on the same gym-attendance outcome.
key_sources: Kautz, T., Milkman, K. L., Gromet, D., et al. as printed in full author line. (2021). Megastudies Improve the Impact of Applied Behavioural Science. Nature, vol. 600. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/megastudies-improve-the-impact-of-applied-behavioural-science

article_title: Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort
citation: Rabb, B., Gardner, E., Pottinger, E., Tallapragada, R., Resch, A., Vorias, T., & Knechtel, V. (2021). Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-for-building-a-virtual-learning-cohort
title: Cohort learning organized around a common theme with guiding values
description: The toolkit's design pattern is a learning cohort of participants organized around a common theme, such as equity, supported by guiding values that facilitators consider when planning activities. Activities are planned with templates and tools, and cohort learning is complemented by project scoping, provider matching, and thought partnership, as implemented in the CBSL pilot with nine K-12 education grantees.
requirements: A common theme organizing the cohort and guiding values to shape activity planning
constraints: Demonstrated in a virtual cohort format during 2020-2021
examples: The CBSL pilot organized nine K-12 education grantees into cohort learning activities around equity-centered strategic learning
key_sources: Rabb, B., Gardner, E., Pottinger, E., Tallapragada, R., Resch, A., Vorias, T., & Knechtel, V. (2021). Toolkit for Building a Virtual Learning Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-for-building-a-virtual-learning-cohort

article_title: Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives
citation: Emily Gardner, Emma Pottinger, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-to-support-capacity-building-initiatives-for-strategic-learning-initiatives
title: Strong equity-centered strategic learning requires equity in the learning and decision-making approach, not only in the organizational goal
description: The article argues that equity must be embedded in how an organization learns and decides, not only in what it aims for. It states that "strong equity-centered strategic learning is demonstrated when equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach." This principle distinguishes equity as a property of the improvement process itself from equity as a stated goal.
requirements: Learning and decision-making approaches in which equity is explicitly considered
target_learning_goals: Equity-centered organizational learning and decision making
examples: The partnership articulated this criterion when defining what strong equity-centered strategic learning looks like in the CBSL initiative
key_sources: Emily Gardner, Emma Pottinger, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives.
