article_title: Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites
citation: Divya Vohra, Patricia Rowan, John Hotchkiss, Kenneth Lim, Aimee Lansdale, So O'Neil. (2021). Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites. Mathematica Research & Evaluation.
title: Build community engagement and stakeholder buy-in, supported by effective communication and simplified informed consent, to sustain school testing programs
description: The report's implementation lessons hold that testing programs succeed when schools invest in community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders. It states that "Community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders are critical to the success of a testing program," and that "Effective communication and simplified informed consent processes can a long way in building trust in testing programs and boosting participation rates." Schools should therefore pair testing logistics with trust-building communication and streamlined consent.
requirements: Community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders
Effective communication with the school community
Simplified informed consent processes
target_learners: K-12 students, teachers, and staff in schools implementing routine Covid-19 testing
target_learning_goals: Maintaining safe, trusted in-person school environments so learning can continue
examples: Pilot sites in the Rockefeller Foundation's K–12 Testing Protocol Demonstration Project implemented routine Covid-19 testing in 335 locations between September 2020 and June 2021, and Mathematica drew on their experiences to identify lessons about acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness.
key_sources: Divya Vohra, Patricia Rowan, John Hotchkiss, Kenneth Lim, Aimee Lansdale, So O'Neil. (2021). Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites. article_title: The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership (Study Highlights)
citation: Herrmann, M., Clark, M., James-Burdumy, S., Tuttle, C., Kautz, T., Knechtel, V., Dotter, D., Smither Wulsin, C., & Deke, J. (2019). The Effects of a Principal Professional Development Program Focused on Instructional Leadership (Study Highlights). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Do not assume intensive principal professional development focused on structured observation and targeted feedback will change leadership practice or raise achievement without direct evidence
description: This principle captures the study's central lesson: an intensive program "focused primarily on helping principals conduct structured observations of teachers' classroom instruction and provide targeted feedback" was implemented as planned yet produced no intended changes in principal practice and no achievement gains. Designers and funders of principal professional development should treat observation-and-feedback training as unproven at scale and plan for rigorous evaluation, since teacher-reported support even moved in the opposite direction.
requirements: Program theory should specify which principal practices are expected to change and how those changes are expected to improve instruction and student achievement.
constraints: The evidence comes from one intensive program for elementary school principals; the study reports null effects for this program and does not establish that all observation-and-feedback approaches are ineffective.
target_learners: Elementary school principals participating in professional development
target_learning_goals: Instructional leadership practices: conducting structured classroom observations and providing targeted feedback to teachers
examples: The study randomly assigned 100 elementary schools, half to receive the program, and compared student achievement and teachers' perceptions of principals' practices across groups.
key_sources: Herrmann, M., Clark, M., James-Burdumy, S., Tuttle, C., Kautz, T., Knechtel, V., Dotter, D., Smither Wulsin, C., & Deke, J. (2019). article_title: Using Kindergarten Entry Assessments to Measure Whether Philadelphia’s Students Are On-Track for Reading Proficiently
citation: Jessica F. Harding, Mariesa Herrmann, Elias S. Hanno, Christine Ross. (2019). Using Kindergarten Entry Assessments to Measure Whether Philadelphia’s Students Are On-Track for Reading Proficiently. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs/regions/mid-atlantic/
title: Other states and districts can use kindergarten entry assessments to track students' progress toward reading proficiency
description: The article generalizes its Philadelphia indicator approach to other education agencies, recommending kindergarten entry assessments as a basis for progress monitoring toward grade 3 reading proficiency. It states that "Other states and districts could consider using kindergarten entry assessments to track students' progress towards reading proficiency." The principle rests on the demonstrated link between KEI scores and later grade 3 ELA outcomes in one district.
requirements: A kindergarten entry assessment measuring early reading-related competencies, and later reading outcome data to validate thresholds
constraints: The demonstrated threshold and proficiency rate are specific to the Philadelphia cohort and may not transfer directly
target_learning_goals: Reading proficiency by end of grade 3
examples: Philadelphia's indicator used a threshold on a two-dimension KEI index validated against grade 3 PSSA ELA proficiency.

Using Kindergarten Entry Assessments to Measure Whether Philadelphia’s Students Are On-Track for Reading Proficiently. article_title: Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project
citation: Dolfin, S., Richman, S., Choi, J., Streke, A., DeSaw, C., Demers, A., & Poznyak, D. (2019). Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project. Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/evaluation-of-the-teacher-potential-project
title: Curriculum-embedded professional development: pairing a standards-aligned curriculum with professional development for teachers
description: This design pattern embeds teacher professional development within adoption of a standards-aligned curriculum, so teachers learn practices while enacting the curriculum materials. TPP pairs "an English language arts standards-aligned curriculum and embedded professional development for teachers", and the evaluation found positive impacts on teachers' instructional practices and, after two years, on student ELA achievement.
requirements: A standards-aligned curriculum and professional development embedded in teachers' ongoing participation in the program
constraints: The evaluated student achievement impact emerged after two years of teacher participation, not after one
target_learning_goals: Common Core-aligned English language arts instructional practices
examples: TPP teachers received the EL Education ELA curriculum with embedded professional development, and were compared with teachers using district-provided curriculum and district professional development.
key_sources: Dolfin, S., Richman, S., Choi, J., Streke, A., DeSaw, C., Demers, A., & Poznyak, D. (2019). Evaluation of the Teacher Potential Project. Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/evaluation-of-the-teacher-potential-project

article_title: Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research
citation: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2019). Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Evaluation Review (online ahead of print). https://www.mathematica.org/publications/beyond-treatment-versus-control-how-bayesian-analysis-makes-factorial-experiments-feasible-in-education-research
title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible when studying complex interventions
description: The article recommends Bayesian methods as a tool for researchers studying complex interventions, because they make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible. As the authors conclude, "Bayesian methods are a valuable tool for researchers interested in studying complex interventions. They make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible." The recommendation rests on the simulation evidence of lower MDEs under hierarchical priors and partial pooling.
requirements: A research question involving multiple related interventions or implementation factors suited to a factorial design
target_learning_goals: designing adequately powered experiments to test multiple factors and factor levels
examples: The authors performed power calculations for a U.S. Department of Education experiment, simulating factorial experiments across sample sizes and treatment-arm counts.
key_sources: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2019). Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. article_title: Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research
citation: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2018). Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Working Paper 61. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible in education research
description: The paper recommends that researchers interested in studying complex interventions adopt Bayesian analysis for factorial designs. Because traditional inference "may require prohibitively large sample sizes to perform complex factorial experiments," Bayesian methods with hierarchical priors and partial pooling make "factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible," enabling testing of multiple implementation factors such as dosages and implementation strategies and their interactions.
requirements: A research question involving a large set of related interventions or implementation factors suited to a factorial design
constraints: The feasibility advantage is demonstrated for complex experiments with many factors and factor levels
target_learning_goals: Designing efficient experiments that test multiple factors and interactions
examples: Power calculations for a U.S. Department of Education experiment showed Bayesian designs reaching a given MDE with roughly half the sample size needed classically for 72 treatment arms
key_sources: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2018). Beyond "Treatment versus Control": How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Working Paper 61. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/beyond-treatment-versus-control-how-bayesian-analysis-makes-factorial-experiments-feasible

article_title: Research Review: Data-Driven Decision Making in Education Agencies. Data Driven, not Data Drowning
citation: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. (2018). Research Review: Data-Driven Decision Making in Education Agencies. Data Driven, not Data Drowning. Washington, DC: Mid-Atlantic Regional Educational Laboratory. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Start data-use design from who will access, analyze, or review the data and for what purpose
description: The review recommends that meaningful use of data in education agencies begin by identifying the decision makers and the decisions the data will serve. It states that "Meaningful use of data begins with who will access, analyze, or review the data and for what purpose," and that data must be "relevant and diagnostic for each decision maker and decision." The principle directs agencies to design data use around specific users and purposes rather than around data availability alone.
requirements: Data must be relevant and diagnostic for each decision maker and decision, as the review states.
target_learning_goals: effective use of data for educational decision making
examples: The review frames its guidance for education agencies around identifying who will access, analyze, or review data and for what purpose before data use efforts begin.

article_title: Implementing Online Professional Learning Communities: Insights from WestEd's Blended Professional Development Model
citation: Jeff Archer, Jeffrey Max. (2018). Implementing Online Professional Learning Communities: Insights from WestEd's Blended Professional Development Model. Reading Apprenticeship at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Blend online and in-person professional development so the two formats become mutually reinforcing
description: The brief argues that professional development should integrate online and in-person components "so that the two become mutually reinforcing," drawing on insights from WestEd's blended model. It positions blended design as a way to combine the convenience of online meetings with the benefits of face-to-face work in professional learning communities.
requirements: Deliberate integration of online and in-person components rather than treating them as separate offerings
constraints: The article states that little guidance exists on how to achieve such integration
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional learning supporting student literacy outcomes
examples: The Reading Apprenticeship Across the Disciplines program blends online and in-person professional development for teachers in a variety of subject areas

article_title: Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes
citation: Johanna Lacoe, Matthew P. Steinberg. (2018). Rolling Back Zero Tolerance: The Effect of Discipline Policy Reform on Suspension Usage and Student Outcomes. Peabody Journal of Education, vol. 93, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/rolling-back-zero-tolerance-the-effect-of-discipline-policy-reform-on-suspension-usage-and-student-outcomes
title: Policymakers should weigh suspension-usage and student-outcome consequences when designing district-level discipline reforms
description: The article's stated purpose is that its findings "should inform policymakers and practitioners on the implications of district-level reforms for suspension usage and the potential consequences for student outcomes." Districts revising zero-tolerance policies toward "more tempered disciplinary responses" should anticipate that limiting suspensions for nonviolent misconduct may not reduce total suspensions and may coincide with increased serious incidents, truancy, and achievement decline.
requirements: District-level policy reform context with administrative data on suspensions, incidents, truancy, and achievement to monitor outcomes
constraints: Findings are from one district (Philadelphia) reform in 2012-2013; the article reports associations following the reform via difference-in-differences, not tested mechanisms
target_learners: K-12 students in districts revising zero-tolerance discipline policies
target_learning_goals: Student attendance and academic achievement in math and English language arts
examples: Philadelphia's 2012-2013 reform limited suspensions for nonviolent student misconduct and granted principals greater discretion over more serious misconduct.

citation: Teresa Eckrich Sommer, P. Lindsay Chase-Lansdale, Emily Sama-Miller, Christine Ross, Scott Baumgartner. (2017). Conceptual Frameworks for Intentional Approaches to Improving Economic Security and Child Well-Being. requirements: Services for both parents and children within the same program approach

article_title: Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief)
citation: Naihobe Gonzalez. (2017). Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Use personalized messages added to existing communications to encourage student participation in advanced coursework
description: The brief presents personalized messages as a low-cost behavioral-science nudge: a small change in how information is presented—a personalized message added to a test score report—can substantially change students' decisions to participate in a program. It reports that "Personalized messages can be a cost-effective way to encourage students," grounded in the finding that message recipients were 49 percentage points more likely to participate in AP classes.
requirements: The message must be personalized to the student's potential to succeed in the coursework
An effort to call attention to the messages should accompany delivery
constraints: The brief notes the messages "might only work when combined with an effort to call attention to the messages"
target_learners: high school students considering Advanced Placement coursework
target_learning_goals: increasing participation in advanced coursework and AP exam taking
examples: A personalized message about a student's potential to succeed in AP coursework was added to a test score report
key_sources: Naihobe Gonzalez. (2017). Small Changes Make a Big Difference: How Behavioral Science Improved Participation in Advanced Placement (Issue Brief). Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/small-changes-make-a-big-difference-how-behavioral-science-improved-participation-in-advanced

article_title: The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students’ Social, Emotional, and Academic Development
citation: Stephanie M. Jones, Jennifer Kahn. (2017). The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. Washington, DC: The Aspen Institute, National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. https://www.aspeninstitute.org
title: Educate the whole child by integrating social, emotional, and academic development
description: The principle holds that schooling should support students' social, emotional, and academic development together rather than separately, because success is "inextricably linked to healthy social and emotional development." The consensus statement presents this as the evidence base for how we learn, framing belonging, purpose, collaboration, goal-setting, and perseverance as working alongside literacy, numeracy, and scientific knowledge.
requirements: Instruction must address social and emotional development in addition to academic content such as literacy, numeracy, and scientific concepts.
constraints: The available text asserts the evidence base without printing the underlying studies, so implementation should rest on the full consensus statement.
examples: The Council of Distinguished Scientists issued consensus statements of evidence for the National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development, published by the Aspen Institute in 2017.
key_sources: Stephanie M. Jones, Jennifer Kahn. (2017). The Evidence Base for How We Learn: Supporting Students' Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. Washington, DC: The Aspen Institute, National Commission on Social, Emotional, and Academic Development. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-evidence-base-for-how-we-learn-supporting-students-social-emotional-and-academic-development

article_title: Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs
citation: Harris, B., Petersen, D., & Wulsin, C. S. (2017). Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/integrating-mathematical-thinking-into-family-engagement-programs
title: Tailor early math projects to a caregiver's language and culture
description: One of the seven tips gleaned from the grantees' experiences is to "tailor early math projects to a caregiver's language and culture." The principle holds that family engagement math activities work best when adapted to the language and cultural context of the caregivers who will use them with children, rather than delivered as generic materials.
requirements: Programs must know and attend to caregivers' language and cultural backgrounds when designing math activities.
constraints: This tip reflects grantee experience reported in the brief, not a tested comparison.
target_learners: Young children and their caregivers in family engagement programs
examples: The tip was gleaned from the experiences of the five Heising-Simons Foundation-funded family engagement programs described in the brief.

article_title: Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs
citation: Harris, B., Petersen, D., & Wulsin, C. S. (2017). Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/integrating-mathematical-thinking-into-family-engagement-programs
title: Help families overcome their anxiety about math
description: Another tip from the grantees' experiences is to "help families overcome their anxiety about math." The principle treats caregiver math anxiety as a barrier that family engagement programs should actively address when integrating early math activities, so that families can confidently support children's mathematical thinking at home.
requirements: Programs must recognize and address caregivers' math anxiety as part of activity design and family support.
constraints: This tip reflects grantee experience reported in the brief, not a tested comparison.
target_learners: Families and caregivers of young children
target_learning_goals: Early mathematics concepts and mathematical thinking
examples: The tip was gleaned from the experiences of the five Heising-Simons Foundation-funded family engagement programs described in the brief.

article_title: Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators
citation: Gregory Chojnacki, Alexandra Resch, Alma Vigil, Ignacio Martinez, Steve Bates. (2016). Understanding Types of Evidence: A Guide for Educators. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: When choosing technologies, base decisions on evidence about which options are effective
description: The guide recommends that educators making technology decisions ground their choices in effectiveness evidence rather than in marketing claims alone. It states: "When making decisions about which technologies to use, you need evidence about which options are effective to make the best possible use of your technology budget." The guide then equips educators to judge evidence quality by describing its four evidence types.
requirements: Access to information sources containing evidence about the effectiveness of the technology options under consideration
constraints: Framed for decisions about which technologies to use and how to allocate a technology budget
examples: The guide orders its four evidence types from weakest to strongest and pairs each with examples of information sources, so readers can locate stronger evidence for effectiveness claims

article_title: A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement
citation: Emilyn Ruble Whitesell. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, vol. 53, issue 7. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-day-at-the-museum-the-impact-of-field-trips-on-middle-school-science-achievement
title: Schools can provide enrichment experiences such as field trips without sacrificing student test scores
description: This principle holds that enrichment experiences like field trips are compatible with, rather than in tension with, academic accountability pressures. The study's evidence indicates field trips "can contribute positively to student achievement," so shifting resources toward them need not depress standardized test performance. It is grounded in a quasi-experimental analysis of New York City eighth-grade science exam outcomes.
requirements: Field trips must be to informal science education institutions for the studied effects to apply
constraints: Effects were estimated for middle school students in New York City on a standardized eighth-grade science exam
examples: The study found small positive effects of field trip exposure on science test scores and proficiency using school fixed effects across 6 years of student-level data
key_sources: Emilyn Ruble Whitesell. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, vol. 53, issue 7. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-day-at-the-museum-the-impact-of-field-trips-on-middle-school-science-achievement

article_title: Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance
citation: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2016). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance. Statistics and Public Policy, vol. 3, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Match causal estimands when using within-study comparisons to validate nonexperimental methods
description: The article states, citing Cook, Shadish, and Wong (2008), that "WSCs require that the experimental and nonexperimental methods assess the same causal estimand." This principle guides the design of replication studies: before judging whether a nonexperimental method replicates an experimental result, researchers must ensure both approaches target the same quantity. The article operationalizes this by comparing to ITT estimates under noncompliance.
requirements: Researchers must identify and align the causal estimand of the experimental and nonexperimental analyses before conducting a replication comparison
constraints: Under control-group noncompliance, standard approaches diverge in estimand, requiring an ITT-based comparison rather than CACE
target_learners: methodologists and education researchers designing evaluation studies
target_learning_goals: valid and credible causal evidence about intervention effectiveness
examples: The article's own WSC compared nonexperimental estimates to the experimental ITT estimate to satisfy the same-estimand requirement
key_sources: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2016). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance. Statistics and Public Policy, vol. 3, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/2015-replicating-experimental-impact-estimates-with-nonexperimental-methods-in-the-context

article_title: Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets
citation: David Blazar, Matthew A. Kraft. (2015). Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets. Working Paper 41. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/teacher-and-teaching-effects-on-students-academic-behaviors-and-mindsets
title: Use measures of academic behaviors and mindsets, alongside test scores, to inform teacher development and evaluation policy
description: The paper positions its findings as directly usable for policy: because teachers affect behaviors and mindsets substantially and differently from test scores, "Findings can inform policy around teacher development and evaluation." The principle is that teacher development and evaluation systems should attend to non-tested outcomes and the practices that develop them, not only test scores. It rests on the paper's findings about teacher effects and their dissociation from test-score effectiveness.
requirements: Measures of students' academic behaviors and mindsets must be collected for the teachers being developed or evaluated.
constraints: The evidence base is upper-elementary teachers and math outcomes, as reported in the paper's summary.
examples: The paper reports that teachers effective at improving behaviors and mindsets often are not the same as those who raise math test scores, motivating evaluation systems that capture both.
key_sources: David Blazar, Matthew A. Kraft. (2015). Teacher and Teaching Effects on Students' Academic Behaviors and Mindsets. Working Paper 41. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/teacher-and-teaching-effects-on-students-academic-behaviors-and-mindsets

article_title: Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2015). Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective. Working Paper 39, Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design school accountability regimes with multiple forms of accountability, multiple measures, and feedback mechanisms
description: The paper's central design recommendation is that an effective accountability regime for schools should combine several elements rather than rely on test-based sanctions alone. It concludes that effective accountability "will involve (1) multiple forms of accountability, (2) multiple measures of educational practice and educational outcomes, and (3) feedback mechanisms to promote the improvement of practice." This multi-pronged structure is offered as the design implication of the behavioral science literature reviewed in the paper.
requirements: Accountability must extend beyond a single high-stakes testing regime to include varied accountability forms
constraints: Grounded in the behavioral literature as interpreted by the authors; the available text prints no empirical test of the combined design
target_learning_goals: Improving school performance and educational practice through better-designed accountability
examples: The paper's conclusion specifies the three-part structure: multiple forms, multiple measures of practice and outcomes, and feedback mechanisms to improve practice
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2015). Re-Imagining Accountability in K-12 Education: A Behavioral Science Perspective. Working Paper 39, Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education-a-behavioral-science-perspective

article_title: Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables (Journal Article)
citation: Matthew T. Johnson, Stephen Lipscomb, Brian Gill. (2015). Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sensitivity-of-teacher-value-added-estimates-to-student-and-peer-control-variables
title: When constructing teacher value-added models, include student and peer background characteristics, especially for districts with many disadvantaged students
description: The article recommends attention to control-variable choice because specification differences have direct implications for which teacher estimates change. It reports that "teachers in a district with a large fraction of disadvantaged students receive lower ratings when background characteristics are omitted," so omitting background controls disadvantages such teachers. The principle applies to policymakers and analysts constructing VAMs.
requirements: Value-added models must isolate teachers' contributions to student achievement to be valid, which requires decisions about student and peer control variables and lagged achievement scores.
constraints: The article notes other modeling choices have smaller practical consequences, and none are as important as selecting which assessment to use as the outcome measure.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts evaluated via teacher value-added models
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of teachers' contributions to student achievement
examples: The study compared VAM specifications with and without student and peer background characteristics and a double-lagged achievement score using data from a northern state.
key_sources: Matthew T. Johnson, Stephen Lipscomb, Brian Gill. (2015). Sensitivity of Teacher Value-Added Estimates to Student and Peer Control Variables. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-sensitivity-of-teacher-valueadded-estimates-to-student-and-peer-control-variables

article_title: Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide
citation: Kimberly Boller, Ellen Eliason Kisker. (2014). Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Five-checklist framework for complete reporting of education research measures
description: This brief organizes complete reporting of education research measures into five checklists covering, in the authors' words, "their study's measures; (2) data collection training and quality; (3) the study's reference population, study sample, and measurement timing; (4) evidence of the reliability and construct validity of the measures; and (5) missing data and descriptive statistics." The checklists function as a reusable reporting pattern that researchers apply when drafting or reviewing methods sections.
requirements: Researchers applying the checklists must have carried out data collection and measurement for the study being reported
constraints: The guide addresses reporting of measures in education research reports, not study design itself
target_learners: education researchers preparing reports of studies using measures
target_learning_goals: complete and transparent reporting of measures in education research
examples: The brief includes an example of parts of a report's methods and results section illustrating checklist use
key_sources: Kimberly Boller, Ellen Eliason Kisker. (2014). Reporting What Readers Need to Know About Education Research Measures: A Guide. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reporting-what-readers-need-to-know-about-education-research-measures-a-guide

article_title: Partially Nested Randomized Controlled Trials in Education Research: A Guide to Design and Analysis
citation: Sharon Lohr, Peter Z. Schochet, Elizabeth Sanders. (2014). Partially Nested Randomized Controlled Trials in Education Research: A Guide to Design and Analysis. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Research. https://ies.ed.gov/ncer/
title: Analyze PN-RCT results with statistical models that adjust for the clustering of treatment students within intervention clusters
description: Because PN-RCT treatment students are nested in intervention clusters while control students are not, analysis must use "basic statistical models that adjust for the clustering of treatment students within intervention clusters". The guide supports this principle with "associated computer code for estimation" and worked examples interpreting model output.
requirements: Analysts need the associated computer code for estimation and a step-by-step guide, using examples, for estimating the models and interpreting the output
target_learners: applied education researchers with introductory knowledge of quantitative impact evaluation methods
target_learning_goals: correctly estimating intervention impacts from partially nested designs
examples: Chapter 3 walks through model estimation and output interpretation step by step, using examples
key_sources: Sharon Lohr, Peter Z. Schochet, Elizabeth Sanders. (2014). Partially Nested Randomized Controlled Trials in Education Research: A Guide to Design and Analysis. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Research. https://ies.ed.gov/ncer/

article_title: Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers
citation: Alexandra Resch, Jillian Berk, Lauren Akers. (2014). Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edprojects
title: Guide structure: define and exemplify, identify candidate experiments, outline critical steps
description: The guide follows a three-part organizing structure: it "defines opportunistic experiments and provides examples," "discusses issues to consider when identifying potential opportunistic experiments," and "outlines the critical steps to complete opportunistic experiments." This sequence moves readers from concept recognition through opportunity identification to execution, framing the practice of opportunistic experimentation as a repeatable workflow in education research.
requirements: Intended for readers weighing whether a planned intervention or policy change can support an RCT
target_learning_goals: recognizing and conducting opportunistic experiments in education
examples: The guide's own table of contents follows this define-identify-execute sequence
key_sources: Alexandra Resch, Jillian Berk, Lauren Akers. (2014). Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edprojects

article_title: Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers
citation: Alexandra Resch, Jillian Berk, Lauren Akers. (2014). Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edprojects
title: When identifying opportunistic experiments, systematically consider the issues the guide enumerates before committing
description: The guide recommends that researchers and policymakers "discuss issues to consider when identifying potential opportunistic experiments" before undertaking one, treating candidate screening as a deliberate step rather than an afterthought. Because opportunistic experiments piggyback on planned interventions or policy changes, the feasibility and validity of the resulting randomization depend on how well the opportunity is assessed up front.
requirements: A planned intervention or policy change must be under way or imminent to screen as a candidate
target_learning_goals: identifying rigorous evaluation opportunities in planned education changes
examples: The guide devotes a section to issues to consider when identifying potential opportunistic experiments
key_sources: Alexandra Resch, Jillian Berk, Lauren Akers. (2014). Recognizing and Conducting Opportunistic Experiments in Education: A Guide for Policymakers and Researchers. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edprojects

article_title: Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data
description: The brief endorses data-informed decision making across every level of the education system, stating that "decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data." It presents this as a broadly shared goal that its recommendations aim to make operational in practice.
requirements: Good data must be available and usable by decision makers at each level of the education system.
constraints: The brief notes that in practice data can leave educators unmoved or drown them in extraneous information, so informing decisions with data is not automatic.
target_learners: Educators and decision makers at classroom, district, and state education agency levels
target_learning_goals: Improving classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement through data-informed decisions
examples: The brief series offers recommendations and strategies for state officials, district-level staff, and system developers to promote effective data use.
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Supporting Effective Data Use (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/supporting-effective-data-use

article_title: Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates with Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control Crossover (Working Paper)
citation: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley S. Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2013). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates with Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control Crossover. Working Paper 21. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Benchmark nonexperimental methods against experimental ITT estimates, accounting for control crossover
description: When judging whether nonexperimental methods can recover causal impacts, the article recommends using the experimental ITT estimate as the standard of comparison. It notes that "Ideally, nonexperimental methods that aim to replicate the results of rigorous randomized experiments focus on the intent to treat (ITT) experimental impact estimate," and that the comparison must handle "substantial control crossover" in the experiment.
requirements: Access to a rigorous randomized experiment providing an ITT impact estimate to serve as the replication benchmark
constraints: The principle is framed for experiments that include substantial control crossover, which complicates the comparison
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate benchmarks when validating nonexperimental causal methods
examples: The working paper develops its replication approach specifically so that nonexperimental methods can be tested against experimental ITT impact estimates in crossover contexts

Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates with Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control Crossover. Working Paper 21. article_title: Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 1 Report: Laying the Groundwork for Data-Driven Decision Making
citation: Kristin Hallgren, Cassie Pickens Jewell, Celina Kamler, Jacob Hartog, Andrew Gothro. (2013). Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 1 Report: Laying the Groundwork for Data-Driven Decision Making. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Assess agency data practices across collection, use, analysis, and reporting when laying groundwork for data-driven decision making
description: The study's interview protocol addressed agencies' efforts in four areas: "data collection, use, analysis, and reporting efforts." This suggests that groundwork for data-driven decision making should be assessed across these distinct practice areas rather than a single measure, since each agency's experience was profiled along these dimensions.
requirements: Interviews or assessments covering collection, use, analysis, and reporting
target_learners: school district and education agency staff
examples: Interviews in the implementation study addressed agencies' data collection, use, analysis, and reporting efforts

article_title: Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief)
citation: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Use correlational evidence on instructional practices to generate specific hypotheses for future experimental study
description: The brief positions correlational evidence on instructional practices as a hypothesis-generating step: additional relationships observed in large studies "can suggest specific hypotheses for the future study of such instructional practices". Those future studies, in turn, are expected to produce research evidence that could inform teacher professional development and the writing of instructional materials. The principle treats correlation-based findings as inputs to a research pipeline rather than as directly actionable causal conclusions.
requirements: Correlational studies large enough to detect relationships between specific instructional practices and achievement
constraints: The brief states the results reveal relationships "largely consistent with earlier research, but not in every case", so hypotheses require further study before informing practice
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement in early elementary grades
examples: The brief reports its correlational findings explicitly as evidence that can suggest hypotheses for future study of instructional practices.
key_sources: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-school-based-rcts-with-binary-outcomes
title: Plan larger school samples when designing clustered education RCTs with binary outcomes
description: Because binary outcomes demand larger samples than continuous test-score or behavioral-scale outcomes, designers of clustered school-based RCTs should plan for more schools than the 40 to 60 typically used. The article's key finding is that "sample sizes of 40 to 60 schools that are typically included in clustered RCTs for student test score or behavioral scale outcomes will often be insufficient for binary outcomes," so power calculations should use the article's logit-based approach.
requirements: Power planning must be conducted before the trial using the logit-based sample size formulas for the planned binary outcome
constraints: Applies to clustered designs with school- or teacher-level random assignment and binary outcomes
target_learners: K-12 students in school-based intervention studies
target_learning_goals: Adequately powered education RCTs measuring binary outcomes
examples: The article derives sample size formulas for clustered designs using generalized estimating equation methods to support this planning
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2013). Statistical Power for School-Based RCTs with Binary Outcomes. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 6, issue 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/statistical-power-for-schoolbased-rcts-with-binary-outcomes

article_title: Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports
citation: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Choose behavioral frequency report formats with awareness that quantification format shapes measurement structure and findings
description: Survey designers collecting behavioral frequency information should treat the choice between "numerically or vaguely quantified frequency reports" as a measurement decision, not a cosmetic one. The working paper shows the two formats yield measurement models with different structure, so the format chosen "directly influences substantive findings." Format selection should therefore be justified against the intended analyses.
requirements: Researchers must anticipate the measurement model they intend to build before selecting a frequency report format.
constraints: Support comes from one experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement; the available text prints no effect sizes.
target_learners: Postsecondary students surveyed about engagement behaviors
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of behavioral frequencies in survey-based educational research
examples: The article compared measurement models built from the two report formats using data from an experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement.
key_sources: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-models-for-behavioral-frequencies-a-comparison-between-numerically-and-vaguely-quantified-reports

article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers should assess statistical power for mediator-outcome linkage analyses before relying on them to interpret RCT results
description: Because the article develops power formulas specifically for exploratory analyses linking teacher practice outcomes to student achievement outcomes in clustered school-based RCTs, it implies that researchers should evaluate power for these analyses when designing studies. The simulated power analysis exists to inform such assessments, indicating that typical RCTs may face power limitations for linking impacts on teacher practice and student achievement.
requirements: Access to the article's power formulas and design parameters for the planned RCT
constraints: Applies to clustered school-based RCT designs using OLS or IV estimators
target_learning_goals: Designing adequately powered analyses of teacher practice mediators
examples: The article conducts a simulated power analysis to illustrate power for these linkage analyses in typical RCTs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2011). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ja-do-typical-rcts-of-education-interventions-have-sufficient-statistical-power-for-linking-impacts

article_title: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2011). Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 36, no. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
title: Report CACE significance findings using correct variance formulas, but simplified formulas may suffice for similar conclusions
description: The article's comparison implies that analysts estimating CACE in clustered education RCTs should base significance findings on correct variance formulas that account for the relevant sources of error. Because the commonly used simplified formulas "lead to very similar significance findings" across the 10 RCTs examined, the practical stakes of formula choice may be limited, though correct formulas remain the benchmark.
requirements: Clustered RCT data with noncompliance, and variance formulas appropriate to the design
constraints: Similarity of findings is demonstrated for the 10 large-scale RCTs studied; the article does not claim universal equivalence
target_learning_goals: Accurate inference about intervention effects for compliers
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator across 10 large-scale RCTs using correct versus commonly used variance formulas.

article_title: The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment
citation: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Consider charter high school continuity when designing middle-to-high-school transition supports for charter middle school students
description: The article's findings suggest that where students enroll after charter middle school is consequential for attainment: continuing into a charter high school was associated with higher diploma earning and college attendance than "transitioned to a traditional public high school". School systems and families weighing high school options for charter middle school graduates may treat high school sector continuity as a relevant consideration, alongside the study's Florida and Chicago scope.
requirements: Applies to students who attended a charter middle school and are choosing between charter and traditional public high schools.
constraints: Evidence is limited to Florida and Chicago as analyzed in this study.
target_learners: Charter middle school students transitioning to high school
examples: The study compared charter middle school graduates who continued into charter high schools with those who entered traditional public high schools in Florida and Chicago.
key_sources: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2011). The Effects of Charter High Schools on Educational Attainment. Journal of Labor Economics, vol. 29, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-effects-of-charter-high-schools-on-educational-attainment

article_title: The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use pretest-posttest designs in education RCTs to improve precision of estimated treatment effects, but weigh the bias risk of late pretests
description: Education RCTs often use pretest-posttest designs because including pretests improves the precision of estimated treatment effects. However, when pretests are collected after random assignment, analysts should not automatically include them: the decision "involves a variance-bias trade-off" that should be evaluated using a loss function approach before late pretest data are used in impact estimation.
requirements: RCT designs where pretest data collection timing relative to random assignment is known
constraints: Bias risk applies specifically when pretest data are collected after random assignment for logistical reasons
target_learners: Education researchers, evaluators, and analysts conducting randomized control trials
target_learning_goals: Designing RCT analyses that balance precision against bias in treatment effect estimates
examples: The article analyzes the trade-off theoretically and empirically for several commonly used impact estimators in education RCTs.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2010). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 35, no. 4. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/journal-article-the-late-pretest-problem-in-randomized-control-trials-of-education-interventions

article_title: An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula
citation: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula
title: Curriculum choice as a lever for early-grade math achievement gains
description: The article treats the selection among comprehensive elementary math curricula as a school-level design decision with measurable achievement consequences: switching curricula changed an average first-grader's math percentile rank by "9 to 12 points" in its estimates. The pattern is choosing a demonstrably more effective curriculum package rather than altering instruction within an existing one. It operates at the whole-curriculum grain, affecting the year's math instruction as a unit.
requirements: School must be choosing among the curricula evaluated (or similarly structured comprehensive math curricula)
constraints: The estimated advantage applies to first-grade math as reported in this evaluation
examples: The evaluation estimated that a school using Math Expressions or Saxon instead of Investigations or SFAW would raise an average first-grader's math percentile rank by 9 to 12 points
key_sources: Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2010). An Experimental Evaluation of Four Elementary School Math Curricula. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 3, no. 3. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/an-experimental-evaluation-of-four-elementary-school-math-curricula

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Establish the integrity of the forcing variable both institutionally and statistically before trusting RD impact estimates
description: Standard 1 requires that no systematic manipulation of the forcing variable occurred, since manipulation makes "the true relationship between the outcome and forcing variable can no longer be identified, which could lead to biased impact estimates." Institutional integrity requires describing who scored, who chose the cutoff, and when; statistical integrity requires a density test or graphical analysis around the cutoff. Both criteria must be satisfied to meet the standard without reservations.
requirements: An adequate description of the scoring and treatment assignment process showing scorers had little opportunity or incentive to change true scores
A statistical test failing to reject continuity of the forcing variable density at the cutoff, or a graphical density analysis without strong evidence of a discontinuity at the cutoff
constraints: If there is both a clear opportunity to manipulate scores and a clear incentive, the study does not satisfy this standard
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Manipulation is likely to be less plausible if the forcing variable is a standardized test score than if it is a teacher-conducted assessment where teachers also influence treatment assignment.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: RD studies must meet RCT attrition standards, reporting overall and differential attrition
description: Standard 2 requires RD studies to report the numbers assigned to treatment and comparison samples and response rates, with both overall attrition and attrition by treatment status. To meet the standard without reservations, "an RD study must meet the WWC randomized control trial (RCT) standards for attrition," calculated for the entire sample or only for units near the cutoff. A study failing this standard may still be reviewed as a QED if baseline equivalence is established.
requirements: Report overall attrition and attrition by treatment status
Meet WWC RCT attrition standards
constraints: A study that fails this standard could potentially be reviewed as a QED if equivalence is established on key baseline covariates, with the forcing variable not exempt from the equivalence requirement
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Attrition may be calculated either for the entire research sample or for only students near the cutoff value of the forcing variable.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Demonstrate continuity of the outcome-forcing variable relationship at the cutoff via covariate equivalence and placebo tests away from the cutoff
description: Standard 3 addresses the untestable smoothness condition underlying RD estimates through two indirect approaches: testing whether key baseline covariates correlated with the outcome are continuous at the cutoff, and testing for discontinuities at values away from the cutoff "where there should be no impacts." Both criteria must be satisfied to meet the standard without reservations; the covariate requirement is waived for the forcing variable itself.
requirements: Baseline equivalence on key covariates demonstrated at the cutoff value (waived for the forcing variable)
No evidence of an unexplainable discontinuity in the outcome-score relationship at score values other than the cutoff
constraints: The smoothness condition cannot be checked directly; the two approaches are indirect
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: Discontinuities away from the cutoff are tested at values such as the medians of points above or below the cutoff, following Imbens and Lemieux (2008); a discontinuity corresponding to another known intervention with a different cutoff is explainable.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs
citation: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.
title: Estimate RD impacts with a statistical model controlling for the forcing variable, an appropriate functional form, and a justified bandwidth
description: Standard 4 sets five criteria for statistical modeling, which "plays a central role in estimating impacts in an RD study." It is "never acceptable to estimate an impact by comparing the mean outcomes of treatment and comparison group members without adjusting for the forcing variable." Studies must include a graphical analysis, justify the parametric or nonparametric specification, support any slope constraint, and estimate site impacts separately for multi-site averages.
requirements: A statistical model controlling for the forcing variable
A graphical analysis with scatter plot and fitted curve consistent with the chosen bandwidth and functional form
Evidence that an appropriate parametric, semi-parametric, or nonparametric model was fit
Empirical support for any constraint that the relationship is the same on both sides of the cutoff
Separate site-level estimation when impacts are averaged across multiple sites
constraints: Meeting with reservations requires Criteria A and D plus either B or C; the study fails if Criterion A is not satisfied, or Criterion D is not satisfied, or both B and C are not satisfied
target_learning_goals: credible causal estimates of education intervention effects
examples: A polynomial degree could be chosen to minimize the Akaike Information Criteria, or a local regression bandwidth justified using cross-validation; sensitivity of impacts to tail observations can assess bandwidth choice.
key_sources: Schochet, P., Cook, T., Deke, J., Imbens, G., Lockwood, J.R., Porter, J., Smith, J. (2010). Standards for Regression Discontinuity Designs. Retrieved from What Works Clearinghouse website: http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/pdf/wwc_rd.pdf.

article_title: Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs
citation: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Character education evaluators should ground measure selection in a theory of change or work backward from an outcome taxonomy, and choose measures with demonstrated reliability and validity
description: The report recommends that researchers selecting outcome measures for character education evaluations first reference "a clear theory of how program elements are linked to specific out comes" to identify the constructs a program is most likely to affect; in the absence of such a theory, they can "work backward" from the report's taxonomy to select appropriate constructs. It further advises selecting or developing measures with demonstrated reliability and validity, given the complexity of character as a construct, and calls for more consistent reporting of psychometric properties across studies.
requirements: Access to the report's outcome taxonomy and its crosswalk of measures with reported reliability of .70 or greater
constraints: The measures presented are not necessarily representative of the universe of character education research nor necessarily the best measures available; the report provides no guidance on or recommendations of specific measures
target_learners: K-12 students in character education programs, including PCEP grantees
target_learning_goals: character development outcomes across cognitive, affective, and behavioral domains
examples: The report highlights misalignment risks it observed: scale items that do not hang together, and mismatches between the construct a measure actually captures and the construct the researcher reports
key_sources: Person, Ann E., Emily Moiduddin, Megan Hague-Angus, and Lizabeth M. Malone (2009). Survey of Outcomes Measurement in Research on Character Education Programs (NCEE 2009-006). article_title: Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes?
citation: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Size RCT data collection for teacher practice mediators according to the power needed for mediator-achievement analyses
description: Because teacher practice mediators are costly to obtain through classroom observations, videotaping, and coded protocols, the report argues power results "may have design implications for the scope of the data collection effort for obtaining costly teacher practice mediators." If power is low, mediator analyses reduce to a heuristic qualitative linking of outcomes. Designers should therefore decide the scope of mediator data collection in light of the school sample needed for precise mediator-achievement estimates.
requirements: Sufficient study schools (about 150 to 200 under OLS assumptions) to power mediator-achievement association tests
Reliable mediator measures, since measurement error further reduces power
constraints: For typical RCTs with 60 schools, power is likely to be limited, especially for IV methods
target_learners: elementary school students in low performing schools
target_learning_goals: identifying teacher practice pathways through which interventions improve student achievement
examples: The report's simulated power analysis computes the number of schools required to detect mediator effects explaining 5, 10, and 20 percent of classroom-effect variation at different power levels
key_sources: Schochet, Peter Z. (2009). Do Typical RCTs of Education Interventions Have Sufficient Statistical Power for Linking Impacts on Teacher Practice and Student Achievement Outcomes? (NCEE 2009-4065). article_title: Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). Technical Methods Report: The Estimation of Average Treatment Effects for Clustered RCTs of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Test the sensitivity of RCT impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes
description: Because standard errors from alternative estimators of treatment effects in clustered RCTs can differ, the report's key recommendation is that analysts "test the sensitivity of their impact findings using different estimation methods and cluster-level weighting schemes". This guards policy conclusions against dependence on a single estimator choice.
requirements: Access to data from the clustered RCT so impacts can be re-estimated under alternative estimators and weighting schemes
constraints: The recommendation is made in the context of two-stage clustered RCTs of education interventions
target_learners: students in education interventions evaluated through clustered RCTs
target_learning_goals: robust estimation and reporting of intervention effects
examples: The report's empirical analysis re-estimated impacts and standard errors for five large-scale clustered education RCTs using the considered estimators

Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report
citation: Steven Glazerman, Allison McKie, Nancy Carey. (2009). An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: TAP's four-component whole-school design combining growth, leadership, feedback, and performance pay
description: TAP bundles four school-wide components: professional growth opportunities, promotion to school leadership roles without leaving the classroom, structured feedback, and performance-based compensation. The report describes it as "a whole-school intervention that aims to improve schools by raising teacher quality," evaluating whether these combined changes affect teachers and students.
requirements: Implementation across the whole school rather than for individual teachers only
constraints: First-year implementation in Chicago; effects on student outcomes may lag implementation
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher quality, support, and retention
examples: Chicago Public Schools implemented TAP beginning in 2007 in K-8 schools
