article_title: The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: In education RCTs, prefer impact estimators that include late pretests over those that exclude them, provided early-year impact growth is not very rapid
description: Design principle for RCT analysis: when pretests can only be collected after random assignment, analysts should generally use estimators that include the late pretest data rather than dropping them or substituting other baseline scores, because the precision gains typically outweigh the bias risk. The paper grounds this in a "loss function approach grounded in the causal inference literature" and conditions it on impact growth rates.
requirements: Knowledge of whether test score impacts are likely to grow slowly early in the school year
Availability of late pretest data collected after random assignment
constraints: Does not apply when test score impacts grow very quickly early in the school year
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators conducting randomized control trials
target_learning_goals: Designing RCT analyses that yield precise and unbiased estimates of education intervention effects
examples: The paper's analysis covers RCTs of interventions to improve student test scores, where pretest data are often collected after random assignment for logistic reasons.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). The Late Pretest Problem in Randomized Control Trials of Education Interventions. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review
citation: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10
title: Target class size reductions at schools with high concentrations of socioeconomically disadvantaged students rather than implementing universal reduction
description: Because class size reduction is costly, the review's background argues it may be more economically efficient to concentrate reductions where benefits are largest. Evidence it cites indicates smaller class size is more beneficial for disadvantaged students, and STAR and SAGE evidence indicates minority, low-income, and educationally disadvantaged students benefited most. The review therefore suggests that "rather than implementing costly universal class size reduction policies, it may be more economically efficient to target schools with high concentrations of socioeconomic disadvantaged students for class size reductions."
requirements: Knowledge of which student groups benefit most from smaller classes, since the efficiency argument rests on differential benefit by socioeconomic background
constraints: The supporting evidence cited (STAR, SAGE) is described in the review's background rather than synthesised in this review's own meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading and mathematics
examples: The review cites the Tennessee STAR randomised controlled trial and Wisconsin's SAGE program as evidence that disadvantaged students benefited most from reduced class size
key_sources: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10

article_title: The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs
citation: Dalgaard, N. T., Bondebjerg, A., Viinholt, B. C. A., & Filges, T. (2022). The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 18, e1291. https://doi.org/10.1002/cl2.1291
title: Hegarty's seven factors associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings
description: The review reports, citing Hegarty (1993), a narrative review identifying "a number of factors are associated with positive student outcomes in inclusive settings": instruction based on student achievement needs, materials and procedures allowing students to proceed at their own pace, additional time for students who need it, increased student responsibility for their own learning, co-operation among students in achieving goals, support teaching, and collaboration among special and general education teachers. The pattern describes a configuration of instructional and organisational conditions under which inclusive placements are reported to work well.
requirements: Inclusive settings must provide the listed supports, including support teaching and collaboration among special and general education teachers
constraints: The factors come from a narrative review cited second-hand by this review; the review did not meta-analyse them as moderators
target_learners: children with special educational needs in inclusive general education settings
examples: The review quotes Hegarty's enumerated list of seven factors in its background section on how the intervention might work.
key_sources: Dalgaard, N. T., Bondebjerg, A., Viinholt, B. C. A., & Filges, T. (2022). The effects of inclusion on academic achievement, socioemotional development and wellbeing of children with special educational needs. Campbell Systematic Reviews, 18, e1291. https://doi.org/10.1002/cl2.1291

article_title: Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math
citation: Catherine Nelson, Julia Kaufman, Kevin Booker, Brian Gill. (2007). Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-grade-math-programs-in-the-pittsburgh-public-schools-a-comparison-of-everyday-mathematics-and-harcourt-math
title: Evaluate curriculum programs as implemented, since implementation similarity can mask theoretical differences between programs
description: When comparing curricula, program effects depend on how programs are actually enacted in classrooms, not only on their theoretical design. The Pittsburgh comparison found no achievement difference between Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, and the authors suggest this "may be related to the fact that" the programs "were more similar in practice than they are in theory." Evaluations should therefore attend to implementation when interpreting program comparisons.
requirements: Assessment of how the programs were actually implemented in classrooms, so that implementation similarity can be taken into account when interpreting outcome differences.
constraints: The article states this interpretation only for the Pittsburgh implementation of these two programs; it is offered as a possible explanation, not a tested finding.
target_learners: Elementary-grade students in public school districts
examples: The Pittsburgh quasi-experimental comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, in which the authors attributed the null achievement difference to the programs' similar implementation in practice.
key_sources: Catherine Nelson, Julia Kaufman, Kevin Booker, Brian Gill. (2007). Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementarygrade-math-programs-in-the-pittsburgh-public-schools-a-comparison-of-everyday-mathematics-and-harcourt-math

article_title: Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program
citation: Jeffrey Capizzano, Kendra Bischoff, Nicola Woodroffe, Duncan Chaplin. (2007). Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Describe the specific elements of an effective program so it can be replicated
description: After an intervention is shown effective, document its specific program elements so practitioners can replicate it. This paper follows that approach: given positive random-assignment results, "this new paper describes the specific elements of the successful program so it can be replicated." The elements documented are those present in the successful BELL summer program.
requirements: A prior evaluation establishing the program as effective, so that the documented elements come from a demonstrably successful program
constraints: The authors state they cannot distinguish which elements caused the positive impacts, so documented elements are of potential rather than proven importance
target_learners: Elementary school students in summer learning programs
target_learning_goals: Literacy and academic skill retention over the summer
examples: The paper describes the elements of the BELL Accelerated Learning Summer Program, which a prior random-assignment evaluation had found effective.

Ingredients of a Successful Summer Learning Program: A Case Study of the Building Educated Leaders for Life (BELL) Accelerated Learning Summer Program. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ingredients-of-a-successful-summer-learning-program-a-case-study-of-the-building-educated-leaders-for-life-bell-accelerated-learning-summer-program

article_title: National Evaluation of Early Reading First
citation: Jackson, R., McCoy, A., Pistorino, C., Wilkinson, A., Burghardt, J., Clark, M., Ross, C., Schochet, P., Swank, P., & Schmidt, S. (2007). National Evaluation of Early Reading First: Final Report to Congress. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Enhance preschool teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments to prepare children for school
description: The Early Reading First program embodies the principle that improving preschool quality on three fronts — teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments — helps children start school ready. Grants were "designed to enhance teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments in preschools to ensure that young children... start school with the skills needed for academic success."
requirements: Funding (grants) to preschools to support changes across teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments.
constraints: Evaluated in preschool settings serving young children, especially those from low-income families.
target_learners: preschool children, especially those from low-income families
examples: The federal program awarded grants to preschools, and the national evaluation found significant positive impacts on classroom and teacher outcomes and on children's print and letter knowledge.

article_title: Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How?
citation: John Deke, Joshua Haimson. (2006). Expanding Beyond Academics: Who Benefits and How? Trends in Education Research, Issue Brief #2. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Individualize competency development rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach
description: Because students differ in which competencies predict their later success, the brief suggests education should be individualized rather than uniform. It concludes that "not all students would benefit from improving the same competencies," so schools should tailor which competencies they help each student develop.
requirements: Schools must be able to identify which competencies matter for individual students' later success.
constraints: The brief frames this as a suggestion based on predictive associations, not a tested intervention.
examples: The brief analyzed how high school competencies including academic achievement, leadership skills, sports-related skills, work habits, prosocial behavior, and locus of control relate to later attainment and earnings.

article_title: Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL
citation: Duncan Chaplin, Jeffrey Capizzano. (2006). Impacts of a Summer Learning Program: A Random Assignment Study of Building Educated Leaders for Life BELL. Washington, DC: Urban Institute. https://www.urban.org/
title: Invest in out-of-school-time summer programming for low-income children
description: The article recommends continued investment in summer out-of-school-time programming for low-income children, because its random assignment study found a well-implemented summer program "can improve reading test scores" and increase parents' encouragement of reading. It names current funding streams such as the 21st Century Community Learning Centers program and Title I Supplemental Services as examples of such investment.
requirements: The program must be well-implemented, as the finding is qualified by implementation quality.
constraints: Support is stated as "some support" for investments, not definitive proof of scale-up.
examples: The study evaluated the BELL (Building Educated Leaders for Life) summer learning program using random assignment.

article_title: Alternative Routes to Teaching: The Impacts of Teach For America on Student Achievement and Other Outcomes
citation: Steven Glazerman, Daniel Mayer, Paul Decker. (2006). Alternative Routes to Teaching: The Impacts of Teach For America on Student Achievement and Other Outcomes. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, vol. 25, no. 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/alternative-routes-to-teaching-the-impacts-of-teach-for-america-on-student-achievement-and-other-outcomes
title: Evaluate alternative teacher preparation routes with randomized experiments before judging their effects on students
description: The article's approach is to base judgments about an alternative teacher preparation route on a randomized experiment rather than on claims or assumptions. It used "a randomized experiment to study the impact of Teach For America on student achievement and other outcomes," measuring math and reading achievement plus attendance, promotion, and disciplinary incidents. This design allowed the authors to report both positive and null findings and to test claims that such programs harm students.
requirements: Random assignment of students or classrooms to teachers from the alternative route versus comparison teachers, as the study used a randomized experiment
constraints: Findings apply to the studied program (Teach For America) and outcomes measured in the 2001-2004 evaluation; the article does not claim generalization to all alternative routes
target_learners: K-12 students taught by alternatively certified and comparison teachers
examples: The National Evaluation of Teach For America (2001-2004) used a randomized experiment to estimate TFA's impacts on math and reading achievement and other outcomes.

article_title: Maximizing Learning Across Investments Recommendations for Funders
citation: Kara Conroy, Kate Place, Greg Chojnacki. (2023). Maximizing Learning Across Investments: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/maximizing-learning-across-investments-recommendations-for-funders
title: Structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing funder, grantee, and community priorities
description: The brief's recommendations aim to help funders "structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place." Cross-grantee learning is presented as a design goal for multi-solution portfolios, with community priorities treated as a party whose interests must be balanced, not overridden.
requirements: The M&E process must be structured to support learning across grantees, not only within single grants.
constraints: The process must balance the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place.
target_learners: Funders investing in multiple learning solutions at the same time
target_learning_goals: Cross-grantee learning about whether solutions work, for whom, and in what context
examples: The brief positions this balancing principle as the purpose of its recommendation set for funders.
key_sources: Kara Conroy, Kate Place, Greg Chojnacki. (2023). Maximizing Learning Across Investments: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/maximizing-learning-across-investments-recommendations-for-funders

article_title: Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance
citation: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/
title: Three-question structure for school performance inquiry
description: The framework structures school performance inquiry around three questions: "1. How are students doing? 2. How much does the school contribute to how students are doing? and 3. What is happening in the school?" Each question maps to a complementary grouping of measures—student outcomes, school impacts on outcomes, and processes driving those impacts—so the three together give a rounded picture of school performance.
requirements: Measure data organized into the three complementary groupings must be valid, reliable, and robust
target_learners: K-12 students in states and districts
examples: The framework pairs each question with a measure grouping: outcomes with how students are doing, impacts with school contribution, processes with what is happening in the school
key_sources: Brian Gill, Laura Dyer. (2023). Outcomes, Impacts, and Processes: A Framework for Understanding School Performance. U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/outcomes-impacts-and-processes-a-framework-for-understanding-school-performance

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3)
citation: Ruggiero, R., Manley, M., Knechtel, V., Place, K., & Shoji, M. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or end in abandonment
description: The checklist's activities are built around "iterative learning, which may mean completing a phase multiple times, moving backwards to a previous phase, or abandoning a solution altogether." Evidence building should therefore not be treated as a one-way pipeline: teams should expect to revisit earlier phases when pilot or refinement evidence warrants it, and to stop pursuing solutions that evidence does not support.
requirements: Willingness to repeat phases, return to previous phases, or discontinue a solution based on evidence
target_learning_goals: evidence-based refinement and validation of learning solutions
examples: The checklist explicitly instructs users that a phase may be completed multiple times or that users may move backwards to a previous phase

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Refine the Solution (Phase 2)
citation: Ryan Ruggiero, Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Kate Place, Megan Shoji. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Refine the Solution (Phase 2). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Treat evidence building as iterative learning that may loop back or end a solution
description: The M&E Checklist frames evidence building as iterative learning rather than a one-way sequence: checklist activities may mean completing a phase multiple times, moving backwards to a previous phase, or abandoning a solution altogether. This principle positions refinement and even termination as legitimate outcomes of evidence gathering, encouraging solution developers to act on what implementation reveals rather than proceeding rigidly through phases.
requirements: Users must engage in checklist activities focused on iterative learning, remaining open to repeating phases, moving backwards, or abandoning a solution.

citation: Mikia Manley, Virginia Knechtel, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). Sample Size Guide. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/sample-size-guide

description: Because rigorous effectiveness validation requires study-specific statistical planning, the guide recommends that organizations treat its general guidance as a starting point rather than a prescription. constraints: The guide's own sample size guidance is explicitly insufficient on its own for determining the specific sample size of a Phase 3 or Phase 4 study.

examples: The guide directs Phase 3 and Phase 4 users to work with a research partner to determine the specific sample size needed for their study.

description: The template enumerates what a complete M&E plan includes: "A description of a solution and theory of change"; information on prior research; detail on how priority communities were and will be involved; the study research questions; the measures and approach for answering them; "Ambitious targets (or goals) for each intended outcome"; and a timeline to carry out the work. title: Balance program or initiative requirements with evaluation needs when providing evaluation technical assistance

article_title: Capacity Building for Strategic Learning: Findings from the Pilot Cohort
citation: Emma Pottinger, Emily Gardner, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Capacity Building for Strategic Learning: Findings from the Pilot Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/capacity-building-for-strategic-learning-findings-from-the-pilot-cohort
title: Equity must be embedded in the learning and decision-making approach, not only in organizational goals
description: The article argues that goal statements alone are insufficient for equity-centered strategic learning. It states that "strong equity-centered strategic learning is demonstrated when equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach." Organizations should therefore examine how learning processes and decisions, not just stated goals, address equity for Black and Latino students and students experiencing poverty.
requirements: An organization adopting this principle must review both its goals and its learning and decision-making processes for attention to equity.
target_learning_goals: Embedding equity in organizational learning and decision making
examples: The CBSL partnership applied this criterion in defining what counts as strong equity-centered strategic learning among pilot grantees.

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Six-element pattern for engaging training and technical assistance design
description: A reusable design pattern for training and technical assistance (TA) consisting of six elements the brief identifies as necessary for engagement: grounding in "clear expectations and common understanding," being "designed around the needs of the recipients," being "developed using ongoing recipient input," being "accessible for recipients," being "delivered by providers equipped to meet recipients' needs," and being "framed as a partnership between the provider and recipient." The pattern organizes TA design decisions around recipient engagement.

Ongoing recipient input during development
target_learners: Training and technical assistance recipients in human services and employment programs
target_learning_goals: Effective engagement with training and technical assistance
examples: The brief presents the six elements as the organizing framework for making training and TA engaging, drawn from interviews with 12 designers, providers, and recipients of TA.

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Frame training and technical assistance as a partnership between provider and recipient, working with recipients to gather and incorporate their input
description: The brief recommends treating training and TA as "a partnership between the provider and recipient" rather than a one-way delivery. It emphasizes "how to work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input on the training and TA they will receive," so that TA is designed around recipient needs and developed using ongoing recipient input. This principle directs providers to build recipient voice into design, delivery, and iteration.
requirements: Ongoing mechanisms for gathering recipient input on the training and TA they will receive
target_learners: Training and technical assistance recipients in human services and employment programs
target_learning_goals: Recipient engagement with and ownership of training and technical assistance
examples: The brief presents strategies such as written TA requests, needs and assets assessments, and TA menus as ways providers work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input.

article_title: Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm
citation: Lindsay Cattell, Julie Bruch. (2021). Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Choose between prior-performance flags and algorithmic risk scores by weighing accuracy needs against cost, ease of setup, and the value of fine-grained risk information
description: The report presents the choice of early warning approach as a tradeoff rather than a single best option. It notes the prior performance system "is just as accurate as the algorithm for some purposes and is cheaper and easier to set up, but it does not provide fine-grained information." Districts needing to distinguish degrees of risk can use the algorithm to set cutoffs matched to outcome prevalence, the harms of over- versus under-identifying students, and available intervention resources.
requirements: Districts must decide which outcomes matter, how harmful over- versus under-identification is, and what intervention resources are available before setting algorithm cutoffs.
constraints: The prior performance approach does not provide fine-grained information identifying students at greatest risk.
target_learners: K-12 students at risk of chronic absenteeism, low GPA, course failure, or suspension
target_learning_goals: Accurate early identification of students at academic risk so resources can be targeted before students drop out
examples: The report compares a prior performance early warning system to two algorithm cutoff options: one matching the same percentage of students as the flags, and one identifying the 10 percent of students most at risk.
key_sources: Lindsay Cattell, Julie Bruch. (2021). Identifying Students At Risk Using Prior Performance Versus a Machine Learning Algorithm. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia
citation: Max Gross, Menbere Shiferaw, Jonah Deutsch, Brian Gill. (2021). Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Use promotion power alongside status and value-added measures when evaluating high schools
description: The study positions promotion power as a complement to existing school-effectiveness indicators: promotion power scores "are distinct from status measures such as graduation rate and college enrollment rate" because they account for prior achievement and background, and they "complement value-added measures by using similar methods to examine additional, longer-term outcomes." Districts and researchers evaluating high schools should therefore report promotion power together with, not instead of, status and value-added measures.
requirements: Prior student achievement and background data, and longer-term outcome data such as graduation and college enrollment, to estimate promotion power
constraints: Developed and illustrated for public high schools in the District of Columbia
examples: The study estimated promotion power for DC public high schools on college-ready SAT scores, high school graduation, and college enrollment as longer-term outcomes beyond value-added measures

article_title: Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC
citation: Subuhi Asheer, Susan Zief, Ruth Neild. (2020). Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC. Maternal and Child Health Journal, vol. 24. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Program elements and practices used together improved academic outcomes for New Heights participants
description: The study's central pattern is that it was the program elements and practices "when used together" that improved academic outcomes for New Heights participants, rather than any single component in isolation. The page frames this combination as defining "a possible roadmap for service providers interested in replicating the program's success". The pattern concerns a coordinated system of school-based supports for expectant and parenting students.
requirements: Elements and practices must be implemented together as a well-defined system of supports
constraints: Pattern is drawn from one school-based program in Washington, DC
examples: The study explored the New Heights program's elements and practices and how their combined use related to improved academic outcomes for participants.
key_sources: Subuhi Asheer, Susan Zief, Ruth Neild. (2020). Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC. article_title: Trauma-Informed Planning Strategies to Help Students Transition Back to School in the Era of COVID-19, Fact Sheet
citation: Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic. (2020). Trauma-Informed Planning Strategies to Help Students Transition Back to School in the Era of COVID-19, Fact Sheet. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/trauma-informed-planning-strategies-to-help-students-transition-back-to-school-in-the-era-of-covid-19
title: Assess-plan-build capacity-implement-reassess cycle for school crisis response
description: This pattern names the five recurring phases the fact sheet prescribes for trauma-informed reopening: "assessing, planning, building capacity, implementing, and reassessing." Because the strategy is iterative, the reassessing phase feeds back into assessing and planning, making the cycle repeatable across the school year rather than a one-time checklist.
requirements: Schools initiate the cycle before the start of the school year
constraints: Derived from crisis response guidance for COVID-19 reopening
target_learners: K-12 school communities, including students and staff
target_learning_goals: Sustaining a trauma-informed learning environment through iterative improvement
examples: The fact sheet presents the five steps as the structure schools should follow when developing their trauma-informed reopening plans.

article_title: Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts
citation: Ellen B. Goldring, Laura K. Rogers, Melissa A. Clark. (2020). Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts. Mathematica, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Utah. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Redefine principal supervision from administration and compliance toward developing principals as instructional leaders
description: This principle holds that the principal supervisor position should be overhauled from a traditional focus on administration into a role centered on developing principals. The report describes the PSI's aim "to help districts overhaul a position traditionally focused on administration, operations, and compliance to one dedicated to developing and supporting principals to be effective instructional leaders." The PSI districts' changes in caseload, training, and aspirant programs reflect this redefinition.
requirements: Districts must reorient supervisor job expectations, caseloads, and training toward instructional leadership support
constraints: Evidence here comes from a comparison of six PSI districts with other large urban districts, not from an impact evaluation
target_learning_goals: Supporting principals' development as effective instructional leaders
examples: PSI districts reduced supervisor caseloads, added role-specific training, and offered programs for new and aspiring supervisors
key_sources: Ellen B. Goldring, Laura K. Rogers, Melissa A. Clark. (2020). Leading the Change: A Comparison of the Principal Supervisor Role in Principal Supervisor Initiative Districts and Other Urban Districts. Mathematica, Vanderbilt University, and the University of Utah. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/leading-the-change-a-comparison-of-the-principal-supervisor-role-in-principal-supervisor-initiative

article_title: The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2020). The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 13, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design the choice architecture of school choice websites deliberately, because small display manipulations shift which schools parents choose
description: This principle holds that how school information is displayed on choice websites — default ordering, icon versus graph versus number formats, and concise versus detailed summaries — is itself a design decision that shapes parental choices. The article's experiment shows that "a small design manipulation... induced meaningful changes in the types of schools selected," so website designers should treat display choices as consequential rather than neutral.
requirements: A school choice website presenting school information to parents, with measurable academic performance data to display
constraints: Evidence comes from a hypothetical school district choice task with low-income parents; the article reports trade-offs, e.g. graphs maximized satisfaction at the expense of understanding
target_learners: low-income parents of school-aged children choosing schools
target_learning_goals: informed school selection based on academic performance information
examples: In the experiment, changing the default order in which schools were presented and swapping graphs or numbers for icons changed the types of schools parents selected
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2020). The Choice Architecture of School Choice Websites. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 13, issue 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-choice-architecture-of-school-choice-websites

article_title: Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2020). Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 45, issue 1.
title: Use grouped administrative data with design-based methods to improve data access for RCT analysis
description: The article recommends analyzing RCTs with grouped administrative data "to help improve data access," using design-based estimators formed as group-level averages. This allows evaluators to estimate average treatment effects when individual-level data cannot be obtained, provided the design conditions the article identifies are met.
requirements: RCT designs of the types covered: clustered and blocked designs, and models with weights and covariates
constraints: Subgroup analyses via ecological inference yield large design effects and are not covered by the tolerability result
target_learners: education researchers and evaluators conducting RCT analyses
target_learning_goals: estimating average treatment effects with restricted data access
examples: The article demonstrates the approach with empirical examples using real-world education RCT data
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2020). Analyzing Grouped Administrative Data for RCTs Using Design-Based Methods. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 45, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/analyzing-grouped-administrative-data-for-rcts-using-design-based-methods

article_title: How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools?
citation: Max, Jeffrey; Tuttle, Christina; Gleason, Philip; McCallum, Diana; Gill, Brian. (2019). How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools? Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Policymakers evaluating school choice should account for its effects on students who remain in traditional public schools, not only on participants
description: The brief argues that school choice policy analysis must look beyond participants. As it states, "Policymakers considering school choice need to understand how it affects students who attend schools of choice, but they should also account for its effect on students who remain in traditional public schools." The brief frames this broader accounting as essential for policymakers weighing charter schools and vouchers.
requirements: Evidence on choice effects must cover both participants and students remaining in traditional public schools
target_learners: students in traditional public schools affected by charter schools and voucher programs
target_learning_goals: student achievement in traditional public schools under school choice policies
examples: The brief summarizes key findings on how charter schools and private school vouchers affect achievement in traditional public schools and discusses implications for policymakers
key_sources: Max, Jeffrey; Tuttle, Christina; Gleason, Philip; McCallum, Diana; Gill, Brian. (2019). How Does School Choice Affect Student Achievement in Traditional Public Schools? Washington, DC: Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ib-how-does-school-choice-affect-student-achievement-in-traditional-public-schools

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research
citation: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research
title: Select the research design that fits the intervention and evaluation setting
description: The article recommends that school health researchers take practical steps to ensure high-quality evidence, beginning with design choice. Among the steps it names are "selecting the right research design for the intervention and evaluation setting, identifying appropriate sample definitions and analysis methods." The principle holds that design selection should be driven by the characteristics of the intervention being evaluated and the setting in which the evaluation takes place, rather than applied uniformly.
requirements: Researchers must consider the characteristics of the intervention and the evaluation setting when choosing a design
target_learners: school health researchers evaluating school-based programs
target_learning_goals: producing high-quality evidence on program effectiveness
examples: The guide frames this as one of several practical steps researchers can take to meet growing demands for evidence and accountability in education policy and programming.
key_sources: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research

article_title: A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research
citation: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research
title: Match sample definitions and analysis methods to the clustered design
description: Among the practical steps the article recommends for meeting evidence and accountability demands are "identifying appropriate sample definitions and analysis methods." In a clustered design this means defining the school and student samples deliberately and using analysis methods appropriate to clustered data, two of the six decisions the review identifies. The principle directs researchers to treat sampling and analysis as design decisions to be made together, not as afterthoughts.
requirements: Researchers must define school and student samples and choose analysis methods suited to clustered data
target_learning_goals: valid analysis of cluster randomized trial data
examples: The review lists definition of the school and student samples and analysis methods as decisions (4) and (6) respectively.
key_sources: Brian Goesling. (2019). A Practical Guide to Cluster Randomized Trials in School Health Research. Journal of School Health, vol. 89, issue 11. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-practical-guide-to-cluster-randomized-trials-in-school-health-research

article_title: Knowledge Sharing through Organizational Partnerships: Insights from the SEED Partnership Project
citation: Jeffrey Max, Jeff Archer. (2019). Knowledge Sharing through Organizational Partnerships: Insights from the SEED Partnership Project. Insights Brief, Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Adapt evidence-based strategies to fit the local context and needs of the adopting organization
description: The brief identifies local adaptation as a central challenge in using evidence-based strategies: "A key challenge for educators and policymakers is identifying evidence-based strategies and adapting them to fit their local context and needs." The principle directs adopting organizations to treat imported strategies as something to be fitted to local conditions rather than transferred unchanged. It motivates the partnership-based knowledge sharing the SEED project organized.
requirements: Adopters must have access to knowledge about the original strategy, e.g., through partnerships with organizations experienced in implementing it
constraints: The article states this as a challenge framing, not as a tested design recommendation with supporting data
target_learners: educators and policymakers adopting evidence-based strategies
target_learning_goals: improving student outcomes through locally adapted evidence-based strategies
examples: Educational organizations partnered with national non-profits to apply lessons learned from the non-profits' implementation of evidence-based educator-preparation strategies
key_sources: Jeffrey Max, Jeff Archer. (2019). Knowledge Sharing through Organizational Partnerships: Insights from the SEED Partnership Project. Insights Brief, Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/knowledge-sharing-through-organizational-partnerships-insights-from-the-seed-partnership-project

article_title: Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government
citation: Julieta Lugo-Gil, Dana Jean-Baptiste, Livia Frasso Jaramillo. (2019). Use of Evidence to Drive Decision-Making in Government. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Leadership support and staff buy-in are needed for evidence use in government decision-making
description: This principle holds that government agencies seeking to use evidence in program and policy decisions need leaders who actively promote evidence use and staff who accept and support that practice. Interview respondents identified "having leadership that supports and promotes the use of evidence and buy-in from the organization's staff" as a factor facilitating evidence use. It complements related facilitators such as collaborative relationships and trust in the evidence researchers produce.
requirements: Leadership that supports and promotes the use of evidence
Buy-in from the organization's staff
target_learners: Government leaders and staff in agencies making program or policy decisions
target_learning_goals: Using research evidence to inform decisions
examples: Phase 2 interview respondents named leadership support and organizational buy-in among factors facilitating evidence use in government.

article_title: Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers
citation: Matthew P. Steinberg, Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers. American Journal of Education, vol. 125, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-school-level-policy-implementation-and-the-consequences-for-suspended-students-and-their-peers
title: District discipline reforms should be monitored for school-level implementation because peer consequences depend on it
description: The article's findings indicate that a district-level prohibition on out-of-school suspensions for classroom disorder produced different peer consequences depending on how schools implemented it: "in schools that eliminated classroom disorder OSS, peer math achievement and attendance were unaffected, whereas peer math achievement declined and attendance decreased in schools that did not fully implement the district-level reform." Districts revising discipline policies should therefore attend to school-level implementation when anticipating consequences for suspended students and their peers.
requirements: District-level policy change prohibiting out-of-school suspensions for specified infractions, with variation in school-level implementation observable
constraints: Evidence comes from one district's reform (Philadelphia) prohibiting out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions
target_learners: K-12 students in district schools, including suspended students and their peers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining attendance and math achievement for all students during discipline policy reform
examples: Philadelphia prohibited out-of-school suspension for classroom disorder infractions; schools varied in whether they eliminated classroom disorder OSS, and peer outcomes differed accordingly.
key_sources: Matthew P. Steinberg, Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline: School-Level Policy Implementation and the Consequences for Suspended Students and Their Peers. American Journal of Education, vol. 125, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-school-level-policy-implementation-and-the-consequences-for-suspended

article_title: Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture
title: Design the architecture of school choice interfaces to nudge parents toward better-informed choices
description: The article's central design principle is that the architecture of school choice — how school information is presented in chooser interfaces — shapes parents' decisions. It argues that "simple design choices, such as  setting the default sort order to academic performance instead of distance from home, could induce parents to choose academically higher performing schools," so interface defaults and information presentation should be treated as policy-relevant design levers.
requirements: An online chooser interface whose information presentation and defaults can be configured
constraints: Evidence comes from a factorial experiment with low-income parents choosing schools; effects on other populations are not established in the supplied text
target_learners: Low-income parents choosing schools for their children
examples: The study tested five presentation design factors, including default sort order, in an online school chooser tool
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Jesse Chandler, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Nudging Parents to Choose Better Schools: The Importance of School Choice Architecture. Working Paper 65. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/nudging-parents-to-choose-better-schools-the-importance-of-school-choice-architecture

article_title: Presenting School Choice Information to Parents: An Evidence-Based Guide
citation: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Presenting School Choice Information to Parents: An Evidence-Based Guide. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Present school choice information in a form that is understandable and user-friendly so parents can make informed decisions
description: Because choosing a school is difficult for parents, agencies presenting school information should ensure it is "understandable and user-friendly to help make an informed decision." The article grounds this principle in experimental evidence that the visual representation, amount, and organization of information affect parents' understanding, ease of use, satisfaction, and school rankings.
requirements: Information presented to parents about schools must be understandable and user-friendly.
constraints: The article notes there is little pre-existing evidence-based guidance on presenting school information to the public.
target_learners: Parents choosing schools for their children
examples: The guide's underlying experiment varied the visual representation, amount, and organization of information presented for a hypothetical school district.
key_sources: Steven Glazerman, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Jon Valant, Alyson Burnett. (2018). Presenting School Choice Information to Parents: An Evidence-Based Guide. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/presenting-school-choice-information-to-parents-an-evidence-based-guide

article_title: Can More Teachers Be Covered? The Accuracy, Credibility, and Precision of Value-Added Estimates with Proxy Pre-Tests
citation: Elias Walsh, Dallas Dotter, Albert Y. Liu. (2018). Can More Teachers Be Covered? The Accuracy, Credibility, and Precision of Value-Added Estimates with Proxy Pre-Tests. Working Paper 64. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Use proxy pre-tests to extend value-added coverage to grades and subjects lacking same-subject prior tests, while weighting estimates appropriately
description: The article's central design recommendation is that states and districts can use proxy pre-tests—prior-grade test scores from other subjects—as controls in value-added models for grades where same-subject prior tests are unavailable, thereby increasing the number of covered teachers, for example "by including science teachers, rather than only teachers of math and English language arts." Because such estimates carry bias, the article recommends giving them "more appropriate weights in teachers' evaluations," for instance via empirical Bayes shrinkage.
requirements: Prior-grade test scores from other subjects must be available as proxy pre-test controls
constraints: Proxy pre-test estimates show evidence of bias compared with same-subject pre-test models, so they should be weighted appropriately in evaluations
target_learners: K-12 students in grades and subjects without consecutive-grade same-subject testing
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of teachers' contributions to student achievement for evaluation purposes
examples: The study used statewide Oklahoma data to investigate whether proxy pre-test value-added models can credibly, accurately, and precisely measure teacher contributions.
key_sources: Elias Walsh, Dallas Dotter, Albert Y. Liu. (2018). Can More Teachers Be Covered? The Accuracy, Credibility, and Precision of Value-Added Estimates with Proxy Pre-Tests. Working Paper 64. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/can-more-teachers-be-covered-the-accuracy-credibility-and-precision-of-value-added-estimates

article_title: Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews
citation: John Deke. (2018). Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews. OPRE Report #2018-63, Office of Planning, Research, and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre
title: Systematic reviews should consider causal validity when deciding whether to include high quality non-experimental evidence
description: The report's title and framing advance a review-design principle: rather than excluding all non-experimental evidence, systematic reviews should assess the causal validity of high quality non-experimental studies when deciding what to include. The provided text states the motivation — reviews "seek to assist decision makers by rating the quality of and summarizing the findings from research evidence" — and notes RCTs cannot cover all programs. The report itself is the vehicle for developing these causal validity considerations.
requirements: Review processes must rate the quality of research evidence and summarize findings to assist decision makers
constraints: The provided text does not state the specific validity criteria; it only announces the report's purpose
target_learners: Policy makers and researchers who conduct or use federally funded systematic reviews of intervention evidence
target_learning_goals: Understanding when and how non-experimental evidence can be credibly incorporated into evidence reviews for policy decisions
examples: The OPRE report itself, titled Causal Validity Considerations for Including High Quality Non-Experimental Evidence in Systematic Reviews, is the artifact developing this principle

OPRE Report #2018-63, Office of Planning, Research, and Evaluation, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. https://www.acf.hhs.gov/opre

article_title: Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC
citation: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc
title: District discipline policy changes require monitoring of school-level implementation, because schools may not comply with bans on suspensions for low-level offenses
description: This principle holds that a district code-of-conduct reform is not self-implementing: schools vary in how they put a new policy into practice, and some do not comply. The Philadelphia experience summarized in this publication showed "significant variation in how schools implemented this new policy" and that "many Philadelphia schools did not comply" with the suspension prohibition, so districts changing discipline policy should monitor school-level implementation.
requirements: Districts adopting discipline policy changes need a way to observe how individual schools implement the change, as the Philadelphia study did.
constraints: The publication reports non-compliance for a ban on out-of-school suspension for low-level offenses in Philadelphia; it does not establish compliance levels for other policy types or districts.
target_learners: K-12 students in districts revising student codes of conduct
target_learning_goals: Reducing exclusionary discipline for non-violent, low-level offenses
examples: The School District of Philadelphia prohibited suspensions and expulsions for failure to follow classroom rules and use of profane language in 2012-2013, and the study summarized here found significant variation in implementation and non-compliance by many schools.
key_sources: Johanna Lacoe. (2018). Reforming School Discipline Policy in Washington, DC. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reforming-school-discipline-policy-in-washington-dc

article_title: The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report
citation: Mabli, J., Bleeker, M., & Fox, M. K. (2017). The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Universal prevention plus targeted intensive goal-setting tier for students needing additional support
description: The program combines a universal tier delivered to all participants with an intensive targeted tier for students identified as needing more support. All students are exposed to Prevention, "which includes physical activity, healthy snacks, nutrition education lessons, and parent workshops," while students who are overweight or obese "also participate in Get Fit, an intensive, 12-week program in which students identify and work on specific goals." This layered structure lets a broad educational base coexist with individualized goal work for a higher-need subgroup.
requirements: A universal delivery setting reaching all students (here, after-school programs)
A criterion for identifying students for the intensive tier (here, overweight or obesity status)
constraints: The intensive tier is limited to middle and high school students who are overweight or obese and runs for a fixed 12-week period
target_learners: All students in an after-school program, plus a targeted subgroup of middle and high school students who are overweight or obese
target_learning_goals: Goal-setting for improving eating and physical-activity habits
examples: HCZ after-school students all received Prevention; those overweight or obese additionally received Get Fit, and the evaluation found BMI reductions for students receiving both components
key_sources: Mabli, J., Bleeker, M., & Fox, M. K. (2017). The Impact of Healthy Harlem on the Prevalence of Child Overweight and Obesity and Contributing Factors: Interim Evaluation Report. article_title: Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2017). Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Researchers conducting multi-armed RCTs should adapt estimation, multiplicity testing, and CACE methods from two-group practice
description: The report's guidance is that analysts running studies with several intervention arms should not simply reuse two-group methods: estimators "need to be modified for the multi-armed design," hypothesis tests across pairwise contrasts require multiple comparison adjustments, and CACE estimation demands attention to its complex identifying assumptions. The principle directs evaluation design and analysis choices in multi-armed education studies.
requirements: Analysts must define the pairwise contrasts of interest before selecting estimators and adjustment procedures
constraints: Guidance is framed for design-based analysis in social policy research, including education evaluations
target_learning_goals: Applying sound statistical practice when evaluating several interventions in one randomized study
examples: The report walks through pairwise-contrast estimation, multiplicity adjustment, and multi-armed CACE identification as the three analytic tasks needing adaptation
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2017). Multi-Armed RCTs: A Design-Based Framework. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/multi-armed-rcts-a-design-based-framework

article_title: Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation
citation: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Align analytic assumptions across methods when comparing impact estimation approaches
description: When evaluating whether choice of impact estimation method matters, the article indicates analysts should align the underlying analytic assumptions across the methods being compared. It notes the design- and model-based methods are most similar "when the underlying analytic assumptions (such as the weights used to aggregate clusters and blocks) are aligned". This makes method comparisons interpretable rather than confounded by differing weighting choices.
requirements: Access to the same RCT data across methods, with the ability to specify matching aggregation weights for clusters and blocks
constraints: Similarity of findings depends on the assumptions being aligned; the article does not claim equivalence when they differ
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators analyzing RCT impact data
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation and comparison of intervention impacts in education evaluations
examples: The study re-analyzed nine past education RCTs, estimating impacts with design-based, HLM, and robust standard error methods and comparing the resulting estimates and significance levels.
key_sources: Tim Kautz, Peter Z. Schochet, Charles Tilley. (2017). Comparing Impact Findings from Design-Based and Model-Based Methods: An Empirical Investigation. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?
citation: Neil Seftor. (2016). What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Education decision-makers should examine what a null-effect study means before making program decisions
description: This principle holds that practitioners considering a program change, such as "switching curricula or implementing a new schoolwide intervention aimed at behavior," should not take a null finding at face value. The brief advises readers on "what to look for in a study that finds no effect and how you can think about what to do next," treating interpretation of null results as a necessary step before acting.
requirements: Access to the study of the program under consideration, so its null finding can be examined rather than accepted at face value
constraints: The brief addresses school or district decision-makers weighing program choices; its guidance is framed for that audience
target_learners: school and district decision-makers evaluating education programs
target_learning_goals: informed interpretation of evaluation evidence when choosing or continuing education programs
examples: The brief opens with the scenario of a school or district staff member picking up a study of a program and reading that there is no effect, then asks what caused the result and what it means
key_sources: Neil Seftor. (2016). What Does It Mean When a Study Finds No Effects?. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Make greater use of professional accountability in education
description: The review recommends that policymakers "make greater use of professional accountability, which has historically been underutilized in education." Professional accountability is one of the four forms in the review's taxonomy, and the authors argue its underuse represents an opportunity as states redesign accountability systems under ESSA. The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis of laboratory and field evidence on how each accountability form motivates educators.
requirements: Policymakers with discretion over accountability system design, as afforded by the Every Student Succeeds Act
examples: The review positions professional accountability as historically underutilized relative to outcome-based high-stakes testing since NCLB.
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education

article_title: Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education
citation: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://behavioralsciencepolicy.org
title: Combine multiple, complementary forms of accountability to support continuous improvement
description: The review concludes that policymakers should "use multiple, complementary forms of accountability, creating a complete system that encourages and supports the continuous improvement of educational practice." Rather than relying on a single form such as outcome-based high-stakes testing, the recommendation is to combine forms so their distinct motivational mechanisms complement one another. This follows from the review's analysis of favorable and unfavorable effects of each form.
requirements: State-level discretion over accountability design, as provided by the Every Student Succeeds Act
examples: The review's third concluding recommendation is a complete system combining complementary accountability forms.
key_sources: Brian P. Gill, Jennifer S. Lerner, Paul Meosky. (2016). Reimagining Accountability in K-12 Education. Behavioral Science and Policy Association, vol. 2, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/reimagining-accountability-in-k12-education

article_title: Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report
citation: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Allow sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation in partnership-based family engagement initiatives
description: Among the formative findings on the viability of leveraging public-private partnerships, the report identifies "the importance of (1) allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation." This principle directs funders, communities, and organizations to budget adequate transition time between planning and implementation phases of family engagement initiatives.
requirements: A public-private partnership structure supporting family engagement, moving from a planning phase into implementation.
target_learners: Low-income immigrant children from birth through age 8 and their families
examples: The report lists allowing sufficient time when moving from planning to implementation as the first of six formative findings from FEIP grantees' implementation experiences.
key_sources: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/feip

article_title: Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report
citation: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Emphasize the supports professionals need, especially teachers and schools, to foster family engagement
description: The report's formative findings include "emphasizing supports professionals need, especially teachers and schools, to foster family engagement." This principle holds that partnership-based family engagement initiatives should direct attention and resources to the professional side—teachers and schools—so that practitioners are equipped to foster family engagement.
requirements: Professionals such as teachers and schools working within a family engagement initiative.
target_learners: Teachers and school professionals serving low-income immigrant families
target_learning_goals: Professional knowledge and skills for family engagement practice
examples: The report lists emphasizing supports professionals need, especially teachers and schools, among its six formative findings on partnership viability.
key_sources: Dana Petersen, Megan Shoji, Adam Dunn, Natasha Nicolai. (2016). Family Engagement Impact Project (FEIP): Phase II Evaluation Report. Oakland, CA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/feip

article_title: Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters
citation: John Deke. (2016). Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters. Evaluation Review, vol. 40, issue 5. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/design-and-analysis-considerations-for-cluster-randomized-controlled-trials-that-have-a-small-number-of-clusters
title: Design small cluster randomized trials deliberately: use blocked randomization, Type I error-safe analysis, and corrected power calculations
description: The article offers best practices for designing and analyzing cluster randomized controlled trials with ten or fewer clusters, contexts where it says meaningful effects may still be detectable. Its stated objective is "to offer recommendations for best practices in design and analysis for small CRCTs," grounded in simulations of alternative approaches. The practices cover analytic choice, blocking, power estimation, and cluster-count planning.
requirements: Researchers must examine which analytic approaches control Type I errors and which design choices yield the most power, as the simulations did
constraints: Small effects remain very difficult to detect with just four clusters
Covariate adjustment for blocking depends on whether precision gains offset degrees of freedom loss
target_learners: Researchers and evaluators designing education and human services studies
target_learning_goals: Valid estimation of intervention effects in small-scale cluster randomized evaluations
examples: The author used simulations to examine which analytic approaches control Type I errors, which designs yield the most power, the design effect of spurious correlations, and scenarios under which impacts of different sizes can be detected with high probability
key_sources: John Deke. (2016). Design and Analysis Considerations for Cluster Randomized Controlled Trials That Have a Small Number of Clusters. Evaluation Review, vol. 40, issue 5. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/design-and-analysis-considerations-for-cluster-randomized-controlled-trials-that-have-a-small-number

article_title: The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Develop a teacher of record definition that reflects all professionals and educational settings
description: The brief recommends that states adopting teacher of record definitions craft a definition that covers every professional contributing to instruction and every educational arrangement, citing co-teaching as an example. A definition limited to traditional single-teacher classrooms would misattribute students in shared-instruction settings. The brief pairs this with implementing the definition through a roster verification system so teacher-student data links are valid.
requirements: The definition must reflect all professionals and educational settings, such as co-teaching.
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Valid attribution of student achievement growth to teachers of record
examples: The brief's key findings list: 'Develop a definition that reflects all professionals and educational settings (for example, co-teaching).'
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. article_title: The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Allow district autonomy in implementing the ToR definition, provided it aligns with state priorities and high-stakes data use
description: The brief balances statewide consistency with local flexibility: districts may exercise autonomy in implementing the teacher of record definition as long as their approach aligns with the state's educational priorities and the state's use of the data for high-stakes decision making. This is paired with the recommendation that states provide guidance to districts on implementing the statewide definition.
requirements: A statewide ToR definition and stated state educational priorities must exist to bound district autonomy.
constraints: District autonomy is limited to approaches that align with the state's educational priorities and use of the data for high-stakes decision making.
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Valid teacher-student data links for evaluation
examples: Key findings: 'Allow district autonomy, as long as it aligns with the state's educational priorities and use of the data for high-stakes decision making.'
