article_title: Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching
citation: Manyee Wong, Thomas D. Cook, Peter M. Steiner. (2015). Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Strengthen short interrupted time series evaluations by adding multiple design elements rather than relying on the basic single-group ITS structure
description: Because the basic single-group ITS depends on extrapolating the pretest functional form as a counterfactual, an assumption the authors call problematic, evaluators should add multiple design elements to the basic ITS structure. Each element limits alternative interpretations, and together the elements provide a strong causal warrant when predictions are complex and results cohere with them.
requirements: Design elements must be chosen so that the predictions they engender are complex enough that no alternative explanation fits the same pattern.
constraints: No added design element is perfect by itself; the warrant is collective and conditional.
target_learners: Education researchers and evaluators of state and national programs
target_learning_goals: Strengthening causal inference in interrupted time series program evaluations
examples: The article demonstrates the approach using No Child Left Behind as an example of evaluating a national program with a short ITS.
key_sources: Manyee Wong, Thomas D. Cook, Peter M. Steiner. (2015). Adding Design Elements to Improve Time Series Designs: No Child Left Behind as an Example of Causal Pattern-Matching. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, vol. 8, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/adding-design-elements-to-improve-time-series-designs-no-child-left-behind-as-an-example-of-causal

article_title: 2014 Facts and Findings
citation: Mathematica Policy Research. (2014). Mathematica's Facts & Findings: A snapshot of significant research results. https://www.mathematica-mpr.com
title: Three-practice school improvement package promoted by SIG
description: The School Improvement Grants program promotes a package of school improvement practices for low-performing schools comprising three components: "using data to inform and differentiate instruction," "expanding technology access for teachers or using computer-assisted instruction," and "providing ongoing professional development in which teachers work collaboratively or that school leaders facilitate." An evaluation brief found over 96 percent of surveyed low-performing schools adopted all three practices, making this a widely implemented improvement pattern in SIG-funded settings.
requirements: Schools must be low-performing schools operating under the SIG program context in which the practices are promoted
constraints: The article reports adoption rates only and does not print evidence linking the package to improved student achievement
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional growth through collaborative ongoing professional development
examples: An evaluation brief on the adoption of school improvement practices promoted by SIG surveyed low-performing schools and found over 96 percent adopted the three practices

article_title: Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 2 Report: Changing Education Agencies from the Inside Out
citation: Kristin Hallgren, Alyson Burnett. (2014). Companion Document for the Strategic Data Project and Education Pioneers Year 2 Report: Changing Education Agencies from the Inside Out. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Four-section structure for documenting agency data-use partnerships
description: Each profile follows a recurring four-part structure: background and context for data use; working with SDP/EP fellows; data analysis and reporting; and challenges encountered and lessons learned. The document states that "Each profile contains the following information" and lists these sections, giving a reusable template for describing how an education agency builds data-use capacity through an embedded fellowship. An organizational chart in each profile displays the path from the fellow's position to agency leadership.
requirements: Site visit interview data from the agency
An organizational chart showing the fellow's positioning within the organization
constraints: Structure reflects the SDP/EP fellowship partnership context and the 2013–14 school year
target_learners: Education agency staff and leaders hosting data fellows
examples: The challenges-and-lessons-learned section reviews difficulties encountered during the agency's partnership with SDP or EP

article_title: Forming a Team to Ensure High-Quality Measurement in Education Studies
citation: Ellen Eliason Kisker, Kimberly Boller. (2014). Forming a Team to Ensure High-Quality Measurement in Education Studies. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Form a dedicated measurement team of staff and consultants to ensure high-quality data for answering a study's research questions
description: The brief recommends forming a team of staff and consultants with the needed expertise to make key measurement decisions. Its stated purpose is that such a team will "ensure high-quality data for answering the study's research questions." The brief is addressed to education studies that depend on sound measurement.
requirements: Team members must have the needed expertise to make key measurement decisions
examples: The brief outlines tips for forming a measurement team in education studies

article_title: Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Develop a coherent plan for effectively using data before or alongside building data systems
description: The brief's central recommendation is that education agencies should develop a coherent plan for using data effectively, treating data use as something that requires deliberate planning rather than assuming data alone drives improvement. The brief states it "focuses on developing a coherent plan for effectively using data", positioning planning as one of three companion topics alongside developing a data system and supporting its effective use.
requirements: A coherent plan must be developed deliberately by the education system seeking effective data use
target_learning_goals: using data to inform decisions that improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement
examples: The brief is one of a series; the other two briefs address considerations for developing or enhancing a data system and supporting the effective use of a data system.
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data
description: The brief endorses data-informed decision making across every level of the education system. It observes that "Most agree that decisions from the classroom to the central office and the state education agency should be informed by good data", framing good data as an input to decisions at classroom, district, and state levels alike, while acknowledging that achieving this in practice is difficult.
requirements: Good data must be available to decision makers at classroom, central office, and state education agency levels
constraints: In practice, data often fails to move decision makers or overwhelms them with extraneous information
target_learning_goals: making data-informed decisions to improve instruction and student achievement
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief)
citation: Mathematica Policy Research. (2013). Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Design education data systems so they drive instructional and improvement decisions rather than drown educators in extraneous information
description: The brief argues that data systems should be developed and enhanced with decision use in mind, from the classroom to the central office and state education agency. It warns that "it is all too easy for data to leave educators and policymakers unmoved—or, worse yet, to drown them in extraneous information, rather than drive decisions that will improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement." The brief therefore treats decision relevance as a core design consideration for data systems.
requirements: Data must be usable by decision makers and educators at any level of the education system
examples: The brief is one of a series offering recommendations and strategies for promoting effective data use by decision makers and educators.
key_sources: Mathematica Policy Research. (2013). Developing and Enhancing Data Systems (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-and-enhancing-data-systems

article_title: Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models
citation: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Researchers using elementary administrative data for value-added models should attend to teacher/student link accuracy before estimation
description: Because unconfirmed administrative data can link "about one in six teachers in these grades and subjects" to a subject they do not teach, researchers using value-added models with elementary school data should verify teacher/student links, for example through a roster confirmation process, before estimation. The paper motivates this by comparing confirmed and unconfirmed links in DC Public Schools data.
requirements: Access to a roster confirmation process or equivalent means for teachers to verify the subjects and students they taught
constraints: Mislinking arises specifically from departmentalization of instruction in math and reading/English language arts in grades 4 and 5
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of teacher effects in value-added models
examples: The working paper compares roster-confirmed teacher/student links to unconfirmed administrative links in DC Public Schools
key_sources: Eric Isenberg, Bing-ru Teh, Elias Walsh. (2013). Elementary School Data Issues: Implications for Research Using Value-Added Models. Working Paper 23, Chicago, IL: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-school-data-issues-implications-for-research-using-valueadded-models

article_title: First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact
citation: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Effective dissemination requires getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form
description: The guide's core principle is that dissemination must be matched to audience and medium: "Today, effective dissemination depends on getting the right message to the right people at the right time in the right form." To break through the clutter of competing communications, researchers are advised to assemble the elements the guide enumerates rather than relying on a single channel.
requirements: Researchers need the right elements: a compelling story, engaging visuals, and a set of electronic tools, including email, video, and social media
target_learning_goals: effective communication of research findings to intended audiences
examples: The guide contrasts past practice—posting a report on the web or sending out a press release—with the current need to combine story, visuals, and electronic tools in one communication.
key_sources: Joanne Pfleiderer. (2013). First Impressions: Creating Newsflashes with Impact. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/first-impressions-creating-newsflashes-with-impact

article_title: What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models?
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: This principle holds that before using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions about educators, decision-makers should account for the likely error rates of the measurement system. The article's results show nontrivial misclassification rates, and it concludes that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators." The principle operationalizes the article's error-rate findings as a design consideration for educator evaluation systems.
requirements: A value-added measurement system whose likely error rates can be estimated from the amount of data available, such as one versus three years of test score gain data.
constraints: The stated error rates apply to measuring teacher and school performance in the upper elementary grades using student test score gain data.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate classification of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The article derives error rates of about 25 percent with three years of data and 35 percent with one year of data for comparing a teacher to the average, and 10 percent and 20 percent for overall false positives and false negatives.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/what-are-error-rates-for-classifying-teacher-and-school-performance-using-value-added-models

article_title: Do Low-Income Students have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers?
citation: Steven Glazerman and Jeffrey Max. (2011). Do Low-Income Students Have Equal Access to the Highest-Performing Teachers? NCEE Evaluation Brief, NCEE 2011-4016. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20114016/pdf/20114016_app.pdf
title: Policymakers concerned with equitable access to teacher quality should attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness measured by classroom performance, not credentials
description: The brief argues that because credentials inequitably distributed across schools are only weakly associated with classroom performance, equity policy should target performance-based measures. It states that those who want to assure disadvantaged students have access to teachers at least as good "need to attend to the distribution of teacher effectiveness, measured in terms of classroom performance, rather than to the distribution of teacher credentials." As policy shifts toward performance measures, information on the distribution of high-performing teachers can help assure the best teachers are deployed where most needed.
requirements: District data systems that measure teacher effectiveness through value-added analysis of student achievement growth
constraints: Findings pertain to ten purposefully selected large districts and are not necessarily applicable to other districts
Few districts systematically collect or use data on teacher effectiveness
examples: The brief analyzed prevalence of top-20-percent value-added teachers across school poverty quintiles in ten districts to inform such equity policy

description: A design principle for education policy: funding decisions that reward districts for identifying exceptional teachers can be standardized at the level of the funding rule while leaving the design of the underlying teacher evaluation system to each district.

article_title: Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials
citation: John Deke, Lisa Dragoset, Ravaris Moore. (2010). Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Collect student-level baseline test scores for covariate adjustment in cluster-randomized trials when precision matters, treating school-level proficiency data as a lower-cost but weaker substitute
description: The report frames a design trade-off: student-level pretest scores "can be costly to collect," while school-level proficiency data are "available at low cost." Because the cheaper school-level measure yields smaller precision gains, studies that need statistical precision should budget for collecting student-level baseline scores rather than relying on the free aggregate data.
requirements: Access to student-level baseline test scores collected by the study, which the report notes can be costly to collect.
constraints: School-level proficiency data are publicly available at low cost but, on average, do not increase statistical precision as well as student-level baseline test scores.
target_learners: K-12 school populations studied in education cluster-randomized trials
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of intervention impacts on student achievement outcomes
examples: The report based its comparison on data from five large-scale randomized control trials conducted for the U.S. Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences.

Precision Gains from Publically Available School Proficiency Measures Compared to Study-Collected Test Scores in Education Cluster-Randomized Trials. article_title: Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2010). Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Policymakers should carefully consider likely system error rates before using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: The report recommends that performance measurement systems based on value-added estimates account for their statistical error before being used for high-stakes decisions about educators. Because simulations show error rates of roughly 25 to 35 percent for teacher comparisons under typical data conditions, the authors conclude that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators."
requirements: Performance measurement systems should be designed and evaluated using hypothesis-testing error rate calculations, as the report does with its OLS and Empirical Bayes error rate formulas.
constraints: Findings apply to value-added models applied to student test score gain data in the upper elementary grades; error rates depend on the number of years of data available.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The report develops error rate formulas based on OLS and Empirical Bayes estimators and applies them in simulations of realistic performance measurement system schemes.

article_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Final Results from a Randomized Controlled Study
citation: Glazerman, S., Isenberg, E., Dolfin, S., Bleeker, M., Johnson, A., Grider, M., & Jacobus, M. (2010). title: Sustain comprehensive induction supports for new teachers across two years to affect student achievement
description: Because the randomized evaluation found achievement impacts only for teachers receiving two years of comprehensive induction and none for one year, induction supports for new teachers should be sustained across two years rather than compressed into a single year. The report states that "two years of comprehensive induction can boost student achievement" while for one year "there was no impact."
requirements: Comprehensive induction components (trained full-time mentors, intensive curriculum, observation opportunities, assessment tools) sustained over two years
constraints: One year of induction showed no impact; no other outcomes were affected
target_learning_goals: Raise student achievement through improved early-career teaching
examples: The evaluation compared teachers receiving one versus two years of comprehensive induction with business-as-usual induction programs

article_title: An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2009). An Approach for Addressing the Multiple Testing Problem in Social Policy Impact Evaluations. Education Review, vol. 33, no. 6.
title: Address the multiple testing problem in impact evaluations using a framework that balances Type I and Type II errors
description: When an evaluation tests many outcomes and subgroups, the article recommends addressing the resulting multiple testing problem with a framework that "balances Types I and II errors". This directs evaluators to choose testing procedures that jointly manage the risk of spurious impact findings and the risk of missing true effects, rather than focusing on only one error type.
requirements: An evaluation design involving hypothesis tests across multiple outcomes and/or subgroups
target_learners: Education and social policy researchers conducting impact evaluations
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of impact findings across multiple tested outcomes and subgroups
examples: The article discusses this balancing framework as its proposed approach for social policy impact evaluations.

article_title: Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues
citation: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ncee.ed.gov
title: Collect and use baseline state test data as covariates to increase statistical power and reduce study costs
description: The paper recommends that studies using student achievement outcomes generally aim to collect and use baseline data, because analyses using more than one wave of data typically have much greater statistical power than posttest-only analyses. Using prior state test results as baseline covariates can substantially reduce overall study costs, since the power improvement allows the sample size to be greatly reduced while maintaining the target power level. Baseline data also help establish treatment-control equivalence and assess potential nonresponse bias.
requirements: Researchers must link pretest and posttest scores for individual students under student-level random assignment, or link individual and/or aggregate data under school- or district-level random assignment
constraints: Substantial effort may be required to link longitudinal data; costs of linking must be evaluated separately for each state because database quality varies
target_learning_goals: Increased statistical power for detecting intervention impacts on student achievement
examples: The paper cites Bloom, Richburg-Hayes, and Black (2005) showing that even aggregate school-level baseline covariates can dramatically increase the power of a school-level RCT
key_sources: May, Henry, Irma Perez-Johnson, Joshua Haimson, Samina Sattar, and Phil Gleason (2009). Using State Tests in Education Experiments: A Discussion of the Issues (NCEE 2009-013). article_title: Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley Chiang. (2009). Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use correct variance formulas when estimating the CACE parameter in education RCTs
description: The report's methodological contribution is to work out the correct variance formulas for the CACE estimator under clustered designs and to compare them with "those that are typically used in practice". Analysts estimating CACE in education RCTs should apply the correct variance formulas when assessing significance of the estimator, measured in nominal and standard deviation units.
requirements: Access to compliance information and outcome data from a clustered education RCT
constraints: The report's empirical comparison finds the variance correction terms matter little, so the practical gain from the correction may be small
target_learning_goals: correct significance testing of complier average causal effect estimates
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator using the correct variance formulas with those typically used in practice across ten large-scale RCTs

article_title: Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov
title: Plan evaluation sample sizes around the larger requirements of clustered RD designs before choosing between RD and experimental designs
description: Because clustered RD designs typically demand substantially larger samples than clustered experiments for equivalent statistical precision, evaluators should assess power implications before committing to an RD design. The report finds that "three to four times larger samples are typically required under RD than experimental clustered designs to produce impacts with the same level of statistical precision." This principle directs researchers to weigh that power cost against RD's applicability when the assignment point, pretests, and research questions make RD feasible.
requirements: Sufficient sample size at the cutoff to offset the power disadvantage relative to a clustered experimental design
constraints: Viability depends on the point of treatment assignment, the availability of pretests, and key research questions, and may be limited for new impact evaluations of educational interventions
target_learners: Students in education evaluations using clustered RD designs
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of intervention effects on student test scores
examples: The report's empirical work focuses on commonly used designs in education research testing intervention effects on student test scores under clustered RD designs
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Technical Methods Report: Statistical Power for Regression Discontinuity Designs in Education Evaluations. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/technical-methods-report-statistical-power-for-regression-discontinuity-designs-in-education-evaluations

article_title: Statistical Power for Random Assignment Evaluations of Education Programs (Journal Article)
citation: Peter Z. Schochet. (2008). Statistical Power for Random Assignment Evaluations of Education Programs. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 33, no. 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Set precision standards for education trials before determining required school samples
description: The article recommends that evaluators discuss "appropriate precision standards" and then determine, for each random-assignment design, "the required number of schools to achieve those standards" using empirical parameter values. This makes precision targets, rather than convenience, drive sample planning in education experiments. The principle applies the article's unified framework to practical evaluation design.
requirements: Empirical values of intraclass correlations, regression R2 values, and other parameters for the outcome and population of interest
constraints: Illustrated for standardized test scores of elementary school students
target_learning_goals: designing education experiments with adequate statistical power
examples: The article discusses appropriate precision standards and, for each design, the required number of schools to achieve those standards.
